### What we’re watching: Weekly disaster update, October 17

##### Hurricane Ian

Ian became a hurricane in the early hours of Sept. 26 and emerged into the Gulf of Mexico after [passing through Cuba](https://www.cnbc.com/2022/09/27/hurricane-ian-makes-landfall-in-cuba-en-route-to-florida.html), as a Category 3 major hurricane.

According to modeling firm RMS, Hurricane Ian [likely caused $53 billion to $74 billion in insured losses](https://www.axios.com/2022/10/07/hurricane-ian-damage-estimate-costliest-storm-florida) from Florida to the Carolinas. Hurricane Ian was the 15 th weather event in 2022 to be added to NOAA’s [billion-dollar disaster list](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/billions/).

**Florida:**Ian [made landfall](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/hurricane-ian-barrels-florida-extremely-dangerous-major-hurricane-rcna49727) in Cayo Costa, Florida on Sept. 28, around 3 p.m. ET. It was a high Category 4, with a windspeed of 150 mph. Ian’s landfall was at the same location where Hurricane Charley made landfall in 2004. Hurricane Ian was so large that the compacted Charley could have fit inside Ian’s eye.

Ian left devastation in its wake with extensive flooding and power outages. The barrier islands of Captiva and Sanibel were disconnected from the mainland after the [major Sanibel Causeway was destroyed](https://www.fox13news.com/weather/hurricane-ian-storm-surge-damage-fort-myers-naples-southwest-florida). There was damage to other bridges and roadways as well, as well as health facilities, schools and water infrastructure.

On Oct. 31, the Florida Medical Examiners Commission said the [confirmed death toll was 125 deaths](https://www.wfla.com/news/florida/florida-hurricane-ian-death-toll-now-at-125-1-new-death-reported-in-hillsborough-county/). An NBC News investigation [tallied 148 deaths in Florida](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/hurricane-ian-florida-death-toll-rcna54069), with 119 of those deaths caused by the flooding, winds and other dangerous conditions during the storm. A significant number of deaths were attributed to drowning. While the death toll numbers are inexact historically, [Ian is likely Florida’s deadliest tropical system since the 1935 Labor Day Hurricane](https://www.accuweather.com/en/hurricane/florida-faces-grim-reality-hurricane-ian-is-deadliest-storm-in-state-since-1935/1257775), which killed more than 400 people. However, the number of deaths was significantly lower than anticipated. [Most people that died were older adults](https://www.nytimes.com/2022/10/21/us/hurricane-ian-victims.html#:~:text=Ian%20caused%20more%20deaths%20in,in%20floodwaters%20inside%20their%20homes.) including at least 30 over 80 years old.

While much of the attention was focused on the state’s west coast, where Ian made landfall, other parts of the state[, including central Florida](https://www.cnn.com/2022/10/09/us/hurricane-ian-central-florida-flood-insurance-invs), experienced significant rainfall, flooding and wind damage. It is important for funders to look at all areas of impact, including central Florida, the east coast and small or rural communities. According to a preliminary estimate released by the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services on Oct. 24, Hurricane Ian caused as much as [$1.8 billion in damages](https://abcnews.go.com/US/wireStory/ians-damage-florida-agriculture-high-18-billion-92056155) to Florida agriculture.

Many Floridians are now homeless. Quickly following the storm, it became clear that the storm would have a broad and lasting [impact on the long-term recovery of lower-income people](https://www.nytimes.com/2022/10/04/us/florida-hurricane-housing-crisis.html). The state’s popularity, inflation and rising rental costs have made it [one of the least affordable places to live](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/florida-least-affordable-state-us-miami-tampa-orlando-naples-rent/) in the U.S. Tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands, of homes were damaged or destroyed.

**South and North Carolina, Virginia:** After leaving Florida, the storm made landfall as a Category 1 in South Carolina, near Georgetown, on Sept. 30. The hurricane flooded homes, damaged piers and knocked down trees along parts of the South Carolina coast. Ian weakened into a post-tropical cyclone but still battered North Carolina the weekend of Sept. 30 with rain and strong winds. Thousands of people in the state were without power, and five people died in relation to Ian’s impacts. Ian’s remnants [caused flooding](https://www.washingtonpost.com/climate-environment/2022/10/03/ian-coastal-flooding-midatlantic-storm/) around Virginia Beach, Virginia, leading the city to declare a state of emergency on Oct. 2, but the city returned to [normal operating](https://emergency.vbgov.com/hurricane-ian) procedures on Oct. 4.

**Cuba:**Prior to landfall in Florida, [Ian made landfall](https://twitter.com/NHC_Atlantic/status/1574678606126583809) in Cuba’s Pinar Del Rio province near the town of La Coloma at 4:30 a.m. EDT on Sept. 27 as a very strong Category 3. This was western Cuba’s first Category 3 [hurricane in 14 years](https://weather.com/storms/hurricane/news/2022-09-27-hurricane-ian-forecast-landfall-cuba-florida-tampa). [Three people](https://weather.com/storms/hurricane/news/2022-09-30-hurricane-ian-live-updates-friday-florida-deaths-south-carolina) were killed as a result of the hurricane.

[More than 77,000](https://www.miamiherald.com/news/nation-world/world/americas/cuba/article266919876.html) homes were damaged or destroyed in Cuba. In Pinar del Río, 68,370 homes were damaged and [7,664 were destroyed](https://www.pressherald.com/2022/10/06/hurricane-ian-destroyed-close-to-8000-homes-in-cuba-damaged-another-68000-government-says/). In Artemisa, at least 9,015 homes were damaged with the majority (7,200) losing some or all of their roof. In Havana, 1,227 homes suffered damage. The power grid went down in western Cuba and then spread across the entire country. The power outage followed a month of [rolling blackouts](https://www.travelweekly.com/Caribbean-Travel/Cuba-tour-operator-says-tobacco-region-hit-hard) due to a fuel shortage. The country’s main fuel depot was destroyed in August by fire after a lightning strike. This is a good example of how cumulative disasters increase the impact on communities.

The country’s tobacco industry was devastated by the hurricane. [France24 reported](https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20220929-hurricane-ian-a-catastrophe-for-cuba-s-vital-cigar-sector), “Pilar del Rio produces 65 percent of Cuban tobacco, while Vuelta Abajo is the only region where the three different types of leaves used in the country’s world famous cigars grow. In San Luis alone, 226 tons of tobacco harvested in August was damaged, local television said.”

Cuba is highly dependent upon tourism and tobacco exports. The tourism industry has been suffering since 2020 because of COVID-19 restrictions on travel.

On Oct. 18, the U.S. government announced that it would provide $2 million in aid to Cuba. [A statement said](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/latino/rare-move-us-offers-aid-cuba-help-hurricane-ian-recovery-efforts-rcna52876) that the emergency relief will flow through the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) to “trusted, independent organizations operating in the country who have a long presence in hurricane-affected communities.”

##### Hurricane Fiona

Hurricane Fiona was an extremely long-lasting tropical cyclone that made several landfalls stretching from Guadeloupe to Newfoundland. The most significant impacts were in Atlantic Canada and Puerto Rico: six days and over 2,400 miles apart.

**Puerto Rico:**Hurricane [Fiona made landfall](https://www.cnn.com/2022/09/18/weather/tropical-storm-fiona-sunday/index.html) as a Category 1 storm at 3:20 p.m. ET on Sept. 18, near Punta Tocon on the southwestern coast of Puerto Rico. A slow-moving storm with wind speed of 85 miles per hour, the high rainfall caused rivers to rise higher than during Hurricane Maria (2017).

The storm [cut power to all the island’s nearly 1.5 million electrical consumers](https://www.npr.org/2022/10/02/1126462352/puerto-rico-hurricane-fiona-luma-energy-power-outages). Hundreds of thousands also lost access to water service. Even before Fiona, there was [widespread discontent](https://www.npr.org/2022/09/27/1125442563/hundreds-of-thousands-of-people-in-puerto-rico-still-have-no-electricity) with LUMA Energy, the company that operates Puerto Rico’s power infrastructure.

According to Puerto Rico’s Department of Health, [at least 22 people died due to Fiona](https://www.salud.gov.pr/CMS/DOWNLOAD/6613), with another 20 deaths under investigation as of Dec. 29, 2022. After Hurricane Maria, there were many challenges in [getting the government](https://www.npr.org/2018/08/28/642615337/hurricane-maria-caused-2-975-deaths-in-puerto-rico-independent-study-estimates) to release an accurate count of storm-related deaths, which include those that occurred directly in the hurricane and those that occurred in the aftermath.

President Joe Biden [visited Puerto Rico on Oct. 3](https://www.nytimes.com/2022/10/03/us/politics/biden-puerto-rico-hurricane-fiona.html), promising $60 million to help coastal areas prepare for future storms. The funding will come from the bipartisan infrastructure law that passed last fall.

Fiona made landfall on the anniversary of [Hurricane Hugo (1989)](https://apnews.com/article/floods-storms-hurricanes-puerto-rico-tropical-01028dac6655ddb5b321f345cf9e9358) and just a few days before the anniversary of Hurricane Maria (2017). Prior to Fiona, more than 3,000 homes still had blue tarps on the roofs because of damage from [Hurricane Maria](https://www.politico.com/news/2022/09/19/hurricane-fiona-dominican-republic-puerto-rico-00057535).

Around Puerto Rico, [community networks stepped in to respond](https://www.thenewhumanitarian.org/news-feature/2022/11/17/Puerto-Rico-hurricane-disaster-response-gaps?utm_source=The+New+Humanitarian&utm_campaign=ed7f8276f5-EMAIL_CAMPAIGN_2022_11_17_02_18&utm_medium=email&utm_term=0_d842d98289-ed7f8276f5-75868082) to needs after Hurricane Fiona, often before any government action. According to some local leaders, the U.S. government’s struggles to implement an effective and timely emergency plan since Hurricane Maria meant “people end up fending for themselves.”

**Canada:** Hurricane Fiona passed directly over parts of Atlantic Canada on Sept. 24, leaving significant damage in its wake. According to the [Canadian Hurricane Centre,](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/world/fiona-causes-shocking-damage-canada-rcna49299) Fiona was the lowest-pressure storm to make landfall in Canada. The [storm wreaked havoc](https://www.reuters.com/world/storm-fiona-batters-canadas-eastern-fishery-farms-2022-09-26/) on Canada’s farming, fishing and fish processing industries, destroying crop land, boats, harbors and fish processing plants.

Hardest hit was the town of [Port aux Basques, Newfoundland](https://www.vice.com/en/article/7k8e9g/storm-fiona-canada), the island province’s main connection to the rest of the country, where at least a dozen homes were washed out to sea. [More than 200 homes were damaged](https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/2022/09/25/fiona-storm-canada-nova-scotia/), according to a spokeswoman for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. At least [two people were killed](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-63011196), including [a 73-year-old woman](https://www.upi.com/Top_News/World-News/2022/09/26/8941664189727/) who was swept away by the water.

Fiona made landfall in Guadeloupe on Sept. 16, with one death reported in Basse-Terre after a [house was swept away by](https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/one-dead-after-tropical-storm-fiona-hits-french-island-guadeloupe-2022-09-17/) water with the resident inside. The [capital](https://caribbean.loopnews.com/content/least-one-death-reported-aftermath-ts-fiona-guadeloupe)was inundated with flooding and there were significant infrastructure losses.

After leaving Puerto Rico, Fiona moved through the Caribbean making landfall in the Dominican Republic on Sept. 19 and then passing close to Turks and Caicos, before moving up past Bermuda as a powerful Category 4 hurricane on Sept. 23. Fiona was the first hurricane since Ivan (2004) to make landfall in the Dominican Republic, leaving at least 800 people displaced with over 50 homes reported as damaged and two deaths. Officials in the Turks and Caicos and in Bermuda said despite telecommunication and power outages there was no major damage in either location.

##### Hurricane Nicole

Nicole [made landfall](https://twitter.com/NHC_Atlantic/status/1590616340934856705?s=20&t=3DNQinuk0RdJtE_MifClqQ) as a Category 1 hurricane on the east coast of Florida on North Hutchinson Island just south of Vero Beach in the early morning hours of Nov. 10. Nicole’s sustained winds were 75 miles per hour.

As of Nov. 11, the storm caused the [deaths of at least five people](https://www.cnn.com/2022/11/11/us/hurricane-nicole-florida-friday/index.html), including two people in Orange County who were killed after being electrocuted by a downed power line. It is extremely rare for a hurricane to make landfall on the U.S. mainland in November. According to Senior Meteorologist Jonathan Erdman, there have been just three mainland U.S. hurricane landfalls in the month of November and [Nicole is the first in 37 years](https://twitter.com/wxjerdman/status/1589646397665689601?s=20&t=UqP8B9gftuAoF4ofi1nI4Q).

By mid-morning on Nov. 10, Nicole had [weakened to a tropical storm](https://weather.com/storms/hurricane/news/2022-11-10-hurricane-tropical-storm-nicole-landfall-forecast-florida-east). Nicole’s large wind field meant that tropical storm-force winds extended to the west, north and east of the storm’s center, including much of the Florida Peninsula, coastal Georgia and coastal South Carolina. Nicole’s strong winds, rainfall and storm surge affected some areas hit in September by Hurricane Ian.

Significant flooding was [reported along the St. Johns River](https://weather.com/storms/hurricane/news/2022-11-10-hurricane-tropical-storm-nicole-landfall-forecast-florida-east) in northeast Florida.The bay front in St. Augustine was [completely underwater](https://twitter.com/TrevorsWeather/status/1590691837475708928?s=20&t=Qa1-e29m6gvpeM3iVtmWkg) the morning of Nov. 10. Nicole brought [above-average rainfall](https://www.sjrwmd.com/2022/12/hurricane-nicole-brought-double-the-average-rainfall-for-november-in-parts-of-central-florida/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=hurricane-nicole-brought-double-the-average-rainfall-for-november-in-parts-of-central-florida) across most of the St. Johns River Water Management District’s 18-county region. Most areas around Tampa [received about 2 to 4 inches of rainfall](https://www.baynews9.com/fl/tampa/weather/2022/11/10/nicole-brought-heavy-rainfall--strong-winds-around-tampa-bay), with some totals closer to 5 inches. A tide gauge at Port Canaveral recorded up to 3.6 feet of inundation above normal high tide on Nov. 10. [Widespread coastal flooding and significant beach erosion](https://michaelrlowry.substack.com/p/rare-november-hurricane-nicole-washes?utm_source=post-email-title&publication_id=913838&post_id=83751943&isFreemail=true&utm_medium=email) was reported along nearly all of Florida’s Atlantic coast.

Damages included homes and other buildings [falling into the ocean in Volusia County](https://www.clickorlando.com/weather/2022/11/10/wilbur-by-the-sea-house-collapses-into-ocean-after-nicole-strikes-florida/). Dramatic footage showed [home damage in Daytona Beach Shores](https://twitter.com/bclemms/status/1590718115783970817?s=20&t=hT6vfQBlFcYDK--fqt_UPQ) as well.

In Volusia County, [at least 49 beachfront properties](https://www.cnn.com/2022/11/11/us/hurricane-nicole-florida-friday/index.html), including hotels and condos, were deemed “unsafe.” According to Volusia County Manager George Recktenwald, “The structural damage along our coastline is unprecedented.” Hurricane Nicole caused [$522 million in damage](https://www.clickorlando.com/news/local/2022/11/15/volusia-county-residents-council-members-discuss-extent-of-damage-after-hurricane-nicole/) in Volusia County alone.

One factor contributing to dangerous conditions along the coast was Nicole’s storm surge, which [peaked at around six feet](https://www.cnn.com/2022/11/10/us/homes-collapse-nicole-sea-level-rise-climate/index.html) the morning of Nov. 10. This is significant due to the very large size of the storm as it approached Florida on Nov. 9. Another contributing factor was that sea level in the affected part of Florida has risen more than a foot in the past 100 years.

Even after it weakened, Nicole still posed a danger. On Nov. 11, more than 20 million people were under wind alerts from Georgia into the Carolinas. Remnants of Nicole [soaked the U.S. East Coast](https://www.today.com/video/hurricane-nicole-remnants-carve-path-of-destruction-up-east-coast-153336389909) over the weekend of Nov. 12-13 and also brought [heavy rainfall](https://www.ctvnews.ca/canada/remnants-of-hurricane-nicole-bring-heavy-rain-to-southern-quebec-and-atlantic-provinces-1.6150498) to much of southern Quebec and Atlantic Canada.

##### Hurricane Lisa

Hurricane Lisa made [landfall along the coast of Belize on Nov. 2](https://www.accuweather.com/en/hurricane/lisa-makes-landfall-in-belize-as-category-1-hurricane/1270391) as a Category 1 tropical cyclone. The 12th named system of the 2022 season, Lisa became the sixth hurricane of the year. Lisa made landfall near the mouth of the Sibun River, about 10 miles southwest of Belize City, at approximately 4:20 p.m. CDT.

Many residents in Belize were [forced to take shelter](https://www.nytimes.com/article/tropical-storm-lisa-hurricane.html) from winds and the threat of flooding. The primary concern was flooding rather than wind damage, with Belize [receiving up to 10 inches of rainfall](https://reliefweb.int/report/belize/situation-report-1-hurricane-lisa-600-pm-04-november-2022) in some parts of the country. The storm surge pushed waters [up to four to seven feet above normally dry land](https://www.washingtonpost.com/climate-environment/2022/11/03/hurricane-lisa-martin-belize-surge/) and engulfed many parts of Belize City.

The country’s National Emergency Management Organization estimated[around 172,000 people were affected](https://reliefweb.int/report/belize/belize-hurricane-lisa-situation-report-no1-4-november-2022), close to 39% of the country’s population. No fatalities were reported, but 500 houses were reported as destroyed, with an additional 5,000 homes damaged.

The impacts on the agriculture sector in Belize were further compounded by Tropical Storm Julia in October 2022, which resulted in the [loss of approximately 2,500 acres of agricultural products](https://reliefweb.int/report/belize/latin-america-caribbean-weekly-situation-update-31-october-6-november-2022-7-november).

By late morning on Nov. 3, Lisa had [weakened to a tropical depression](https://www.sun-sentinel.com/news/weather/hurricane/fl-ne-hurricane-martin-lisa-caribbean-mexico-newfoundland-thursday-20221103-smwnbejymjaxnnhvoz4e57nv6q-story.html) over Mexico.

##### Housing

Many people struggle to find safe and affordable housing following a hurricane, particularly those from poor and marginalized backgrounds. For example, Hurricane Ida [exacerbated an affordable housing crisis](https://www.ksla.com/2021/09/17/housing-concerns-grow-demand-is-high-supply-is-low-following-hurricane-ida/) in New Orleans as the housing supply post-disaster was low, but demand was high. This is even more true after Hurricanes Fiona and Ian.

Houses that are only partially damaged may need to have mucking and gutting done, clean-up and tarping of roofs.

Housing prices in southern Florida have been increasing, limiting the ability of renters and people living in poverty to find housing. Florida was [already experiencing a housing crunch](https://www.nytimes.com/2022/10/04/us/florida-hurricane-housing-crisis.html) before the hurricane, which will make a recovery hardest on people already struggling to make ends meet. Numerous insurance companies have closed and therefore, finding new insurance after a storm may be even more difficult.

Linked to this are income support programs. Many of the damaged homes were among [low and middle](https://www.nytimes.com/2022/10/04/us/florida-hurricane-housing-crisis.html) income residents and/or [retirees on fixed incomes](https://www.politico.com/news/2022/10/10/ian-cracks-floridians-nest-eggs-00060759). Renters are often subjected to unfair evictions after disasters, as landlords realize they can increase rents due to the shortages. Wealthier homeowners likely have insurance that will also allow them to rent temporary housing during repairs, further restricting the rental market.

##### Mobile and manufactured homes

While housing overall will be a significant need, there are hundreds of thousands of mobile homes in Florida. In Manatee County, the [most damage was found in manufactured housing](https://www.heraldtribune.com/story/weather/hurricane/2022/10/13/manatee-county-map-hurricane-ian-major-damage-manufactured-homes/10478211002/).

Before Hurricane Ian, there were 1,200 mobile home developments along Southwest Florida’s coastline. According to [NPR](https://www.npr.org/2022/10/08/1127689323/hurricane-ian-highlighted-the-vulnerabilities-of-older-mobile-homes), “Of 822,000 mobile and manufactured homes in the state, almost two-thirds of them are pre-1994 vintage.” Hurricane Andrew’s impact on mobile and manufactured homes was so significant that the federal government tightened the wind standards just two years later. In Park Hill Estates in Punta Gorda, the homes are all build to post-1994 standards because they were destroyed during 2004’s Hurricane Charley. As a result, 99% of the homes made it through the storm, with the occasional siding, skirting or roof damage.

[CDP hosted a webinar](https://disasterphilanthropy.org/events/mobile-homes-and-disaster-understanding-risks-and-opportunities/) on Oct. 13, 2022, on mobile housing during disasters that offers advice for funders on supporting these communities.

##### Economic and community development

The compounding effects of COVID-19 delayed recovery from storms in 2021. Livelihoods support and investing in local economies will be needed for people to recover fully. The extensive power outages led to increased costs for individuals and businesses alike. Florida and Puerto Rico are strong tourist destinations, and the storms have significantly impacted future revenue.

##### Health and behavioral health

Research shows that hurricanes cause and exacerbate [multiple diseases](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7967478/#:~:text=Hurricanes%20are%20shown%20to%20cause,years%20following%20the%20hurricane%20impact.). While many health impacts peak within six months following hurricanes, chronic diseases continue to occur for years. Hurricanes also inflict harm to the [mental health](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/news/hurricanes-take-heavy-toll-mental-health-survivors#:~:text=According%20to%20their%20work%2C%20exposure,if%20they%20are%20in%20recovery.) of people in their paths.

At least three suicides and one murder were linked to Hurricane Ian in Florida. These numbers are likely to increase as people realize they are not going to be able to rebuild or suffer additional impacts from the storm including loss of family and friends (due to death or displacement), loss of income, loss of housing, etc. Two of the suicides were linked to men in their 70s who saw the [destruction](https://www.foxweather.com/weather-news/most-hurricane-ian-deaths-in-florida-were-drownings-data-shows) of their housing and could not cope.

For Fiona, there was a high rate of pre-existing disability in Puerto Rico.  According to the most recent data from the 2019 [American Community Survey](https://www.disabilitystatistics.org/reports/2019/English/HTML/report2019.cfm?fips=2072000&html_year=2019&subButton=Get+HTML#summary) the prevalence of disabilities was:

*   21.7% for persons of all ages
*   0.8% for persons ages 4 and under
*   11.7% for persons ages 5 to 15
*   9.1% for persons ages 16 to 20
*   16.6% for persons ages 21 to 64
*   37% for persons ages 65 to 74
*   61.9% for persons ages 75+

Residents are unable to access federal disability income support benefits, so [many disabled residents](https://www.cbpp.org/research/aid-to-the-aged-blind-and-disabled) live in poverty on the island.Additional health care support will be needed to assist this population with recovery (as well as additional resources to rebuild, as their disability may limit their own participation in the reconstruction).

##### Government recovery assistance

Once again, infrastructure spending will be an important area. While the federal government has promised to support recovery for U.S.-based disasters, there is still a 25% cost-share that some local governments may have issues funding. In other countries, there may not be the structural funding programs that the U.S. has in place. That is one area that philanthropy can be of assistance with infrastructure spending.

[Technical assistance and oversight](https://www.nytimes.com/2022/09/19/climate/puerto-rico-hurricane-fiona.html) from philanthropy may also be helpful. As of August 2022, Puerto Rico had only spent 19% ($5.3 billion) of the post-Maria (and Irma) recovery dollars [funded by FEMA](https://transportation.house.gov/committee-activity/hearings/recovery-update-status-of-fema-recovery-efforts-in-puerto-rico-and-us-virgin-islands-5-years-after-hurricanes-irma-and-maria) for 2017. Most of that money – about 81% – went towards debris removal and other emergency response measures. Road and utility repairs remain undone.

##### Navigating assistance processes

Disaster assistance may be available in various forms and from different sources. People will need help navigating a complicated assistance process, particularly undocumented people and people whose first language is not English.

A recently released study from the [U.S. Commission on Human Rights](https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/2022/09/21/hurricane-fema-poor-disabled-immigrants/) found that FEMA did not equitably serve at-risk populations including people with disabilities, people living in poverty and English as a second language speakers during Hurricanes Harvey or Maria in 2017.

###### Philanthropic and government support

In 2020, the Center for Disaster Philanthropy (CDP) removed the “annual” designation from its Atlantic Hurricane Season Recovery Fund to allow a broader focus on the full spectrum of the disaster cycle.

The following are examples of grants awarded through this fund:

*   **CDP** awarded $50,000 to [**Culture Aid NOLA**](https://www.cultureaidnola.org/) in 2022 to support “July Supply,” an event aimed at preparing the families of New Orleans for the coming most-active months of the season hurricane season.
*   [**SBP**](https://sbpusa.org/) received a $150,000 grant in 2021 to support their [SHARE](https://sbpusa.org/what-we-do/share) program and serve at least nine vulnerable families in southwest Louisiana by rebuilding homes damaged or destroyed by Hurricanes Laura and Sally, thus shrinking the time between disaster and their recovery. SBP will leverage CDP’s support against other funding sources and community resources to serve families through its rebuilding program and SHARE grant program administered by SBP that distributes per-project gap funding to nonprofit rebuilding partners active in the area. The [**Fuller Center for Housing**](https://fullercenter.org/) and [**All Hands and Hearts**](https://www.allhandsandhearts.org/) received $50,000 each from SBP via this grant to support their work. SBP will be implementing its SHARE program again in response to Hurricane Ida.
*   [**GER3 (Global Emergency Relief, Recovery and Reconstruction)**](http://www.ger3.org/) received a $50,000 grant in partnership with Google to provide critical recovery services to highly vulnerable and severely affected communities in the North Zone of Honduras following Hurricanes Eta and Iota, with the potential transition into reconstruction efforts. With the aim of removing debris and cleaning 200+ structures across two communities, the community-led project approach will integrate local team members and cash-for-work opportunities while focusing on building back better, increasing sustainability and resiliency.

Hurricane Ian:

*   In Florida, an emergency declaration ([EM-3584](https://www.fema.gov/disaster/3584)) was issued on Sept. 23. A disaster declaration ([DR-4673](https://www.fema.gov/disaster/4673)) was announced after landfall. FEMA approved 368,480 Individual Assistance applications for $871,257,134 as of Jan. 9, 2023. On Sept. 30, a disaster declaration ([DR-4675](https://www.fema.gov/disaster/4675)) was announced for the Seminole Tribe of Florida. As of Dec. 22, FEMA had approved nine Individual Assistance applications for $17,410.
*   In North Carolina, an emergency declaration ([EM-3586](https://www.fema.gov/disaster/3586)) was issued on Oct. 1. As of Dec. 30, more than $1.32 million in total public assistance grant dollars were obligated.
*   In South Carolina, an emergency declaration ([EM-3585](https://www.fema.gov/disaster/3585)) was issued on Sept. 25. A disaster declaration ([DR-4677](https://www.fema.gov/disaster/4677)) was announced on Nov. 21. FEMA approved 949 Individual Assistance applications for $1,929,270 as of Jan. 9, 2023.

Hurricane Fiona:

*   In Puerto Rico, an emergency declaration ([EM-3583](https://www.fema.gov/disaster/3583)) was issued on Sept. 18. A disaster declaration ([DR-4671](https://www.fema.gov/disaster/4671)) was announced on Sept. 21. FEMA approved 723,005 Individual Assistance applications for $593,995,487 as of Jan. 9, 2023. More than $92.38 million in public assistance grant dollars were obligated.

Hurricane Nicole:

*   On Nov. 9, President Biden [approved an emergency declaration](https://www.fema.gov/press-release/20221109/president-joseph-r-biden-jr-approves-emergency-declaration-florida) for Florida. On Nov. 10, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis [declared a state of emergency](https://www.flgov.com/2022/11/10/memo-executive-order-22-256-amending-executive-order-22-253-emergency-management-hurricane-nicole/) covering all 67 Florida counties. On Dec. 13, a disaster declaration ([DR-4680](https://www.fema.gov/disaster/4680/designated-areas)) was issued designating six counties for Individual Assistance and Public Assistance for many counties. As of Jan. 11, 2023, 527 Individual Assistance applications were approved for $2,390,778.

In France, [President Emmanuel Macron](https://www.wionews.com/world/after-storm-fiona-hits-guadeloupe-macron-says-france-to-recognise-state-of-natural-disaster-517475) recognized a state of disaster for Guadeloupe and opened a special relief fund.

In Canada, the federal and provincial governments said they would [support people and businesses](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-ottawa-to-deliver-financial-aid-for-uninsured-people-affected-by-post/) who did not have sufficient insurance or were considered to be uninsurable by insurance companies. On Oct. 4, Prime Minister Justin Trudeau [announced a $300 million recovery fund](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/trudeau-fiona-recovery-package-atlantic-1.6605351) for Atlantic Canadians.

By Mack McPherson January 18, 2023

[![Image 3: 2022 hurricane season has come and gone](https://api.army.mil/e2/c/images/2023/01/18/97ed0b87/size0-full.jpg)](https://api.army.mil/e2/c/images/2023/01/18/97ed0b87/original.jpg)

 The 2022 Atlantic hurricane season officially ended on Nov. 30. The impact of Hurricanes Ian, Nicole and Fiona, which brought extensive damage to Florida’s coast and Puerto Rico respectively, continue to be felt long after the season is over. In total, this hurricane season produced 14 named storms, of which eight became hurricanes and two intensified to major hurricanes with winds reaching 111 mph or greater. An average hurricane season has 14 named storms, seven hurricanes and three major hurricanes. (Graphic courtesy of National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration)  (Photo Credit: Courtesy)[View original](https://api.army.mil/e2/c/images/2023/01/18/97ed0b87/original.jpg "View original")

The 2022 Atlantic hurricane season officially ended on Nov. 30. Regardless, the impact of Hurricanes Ian, Nicole and Fiona, which brought extensive damage to Florida’s coast and Puerto Rico, continue to be felt.

In total, this hurricane season produced 14 named storms that reached 39 miles per hour or greater. Eight of the storms became hurricanes with winds of 74 mph or greater and two intensified into major hurricanes with winds reaching 111 mph or greater. An average hurricane season has 14 named storms, seven hurricanes and three major hurricanes.

The 2022 season saw three hurricane landfalls along the coast of the United States mainland. Hurricane Ian made landfall first as a Category 4 storm in Cayo Costa, Florida, and again as a Category 1 in Georgetown, South Carolina. As a Category 4 with 150 mph maximum sustained winds, Hurricane Ian tied for the fifth-strongest hurricane ever to make landfall in the U.S. Hurricane Nicole made landfall as a Category 1 in north Hutchinson Island, Florida.

Hurricane Fiona made landfall outside of the mainland U.S. as a Category 1 near Punta Tocon, Puerto Rico.

This unique season was defined by a rare mid-season pause in storms that scientists preliminarily believe was caused by increased wind shear and suppressed atmospheric moisture high over the Atlantic Ocean. After a quiet period in August, activity ramped up in September with seven named storms, including the two major hurricanes, Fiona and Ian. The season also included a rare late-season storm with Hurricane Nicole making landfall on November 10 along the east coast of Florida.

National Hurricane Center forecasts were aided by the experimental peak storm surge graphic, which allowed forecasters to more accurately communicate the severity of expected storm surge levels produced by landfalling storms, such as Hurricane Ian. Additionally, NOAA’s intensity forecasts showed Hurricane Ian as a major hurricane impacting the coast of Florida from the initial advisory on Sept. 23 through landfall five days later. This advanced lead time gave those in threatened areas more time to prepare and respond.

The 2022 seasonal activity fell within NOAA’s predicted ranges for named storms and hurricanes in both of their pre-season outlook and updated outlook. La Niña conditions remained robust throughout the season while the West African Monsoon was only slightly above normal, which both largely aligned with conditions anticipated by the team at NOAA.

NOAA’s hurricane research and response.

This season, NOAA Hurricane Hunter aircraft flew over 582 mission hours to collect atmospheric data that is critical to hurricane forecasting and research, passing through the eye of a hurricane 65 times and deploying over 1,700 scientific instruments. NOAA’s Gulfstream IV-SP also flew a research mission from Cabo Verde, Africa, in August. This historic mission was the furthest east NOAA’s Hurricane Hunter airplanes have flown to investigate a developing storm.

Another major first included the successful launch of the Altius 600 small uncrewed aircraft system by from NOAA’s Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Lab. Scientists launched the instrument from NOAA’s P-3 Hurricane Hunter into the core of Hurricane Ian hours before landfall, transmitting back data of wind speeds as high as 216 mph at an altitude of 2,150 feet.

NOAA's National Ocean Service captured thousands of aerial overflight images after Hurricane Ian. The images helped identify and record more than 6,200 potential pollution risks and assisted the U.S. Coast Guard in clearing pollution from the environment and facilitating marine debris cleanup efforts. A NOAA King Air and Twin Otter aircraft flew over 41 mission hours to support aerial imagery collection for emergency response after Hurricanes Ian and Nicole.

Forecasters and researchers relied on this invaluable data coupled with NOAA’s advanced geostationary and polar-orbiting weather satellites, NOAA's weather buoys and other sources before, during and after storms throughout this destructive hurricane season.

While the 2022 season is drawing to a close, now is not the time to let your guard down. The 2023 hurricane season will officially begin on June 1. Let’s take the time to ensure your family is Weather-Ready for the season ahead. NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center, a division of the National Weather Service, will issue its initial 2023 seasonal outlook in May.

There is much to be done as we prepare for the 2023 Hurricane Season, identifying stay-back personnel (Fort Stewart-Hunter Army Airfield numbers still remains high); two Force Protection Exercises for Garrison and 3rd Infantry Division to plan; a Hurricane Plan Review; and command post exercises with a new system to replace WebEOC to be learned by all Fort Stewart-Hunter Army Airfield garrison Emergency Operation Center members.

It's never too early to start looking over your family plans now for the 2023 Hurricane Season.

This advanced lead time gave those in threatened areas more time to prepare and respond.

The 2022 seasonal activity fell within NOAA’s predicted ranges for named storms and hurricanes in both of their pre-season outlook and updated outlook. La Niña conditions remained robust throughout the season while the West African Monsoon was only slightly above normal, which both largely aligned with conditions anticipated by the team at NOAA.

NOAA’s hurricane research and response.

This season, NOAA Hurricane Hunter aircraft flew over 582 mission hours to collect atmospheric data that is critical to hurricane forecasting and research, passing through the eye of a hurricane 65 times and deploying over 1,700 scientific instruments. NOAA’s Gulfstream IV-SP also flew a research mission from Cabo Verde, Africa, in August. This historic mission was the furthest east NOAA’s Hurricane Hunter airplanes have flown to investigate a developing storm.

Another major first included the successful launch of the Altius 600 small uncrewed aircraft system by from NOAA’s Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Lab. Scientists launched the instrument from NOAA’s P-3 Hurricane Hunter into the core of Hurricane Ian hours before landfall, transmitting back data of wind speeds as high as 216 mph at an altitude of 2,150 feet.

NOAA's National Ocean Service captured thousands of aerial overflight images after Hurricane Ian. The images helped identify and record more than 6,200 potential pollution risks and assisted the U.S. Coast Guard in clearing pollution from the environment and facilitating marine debris cleanup efforts. A NOAA King Air and Twin Otter aircraft flew over 41 mission hours to support aerial imagery collection for emergency response after Hurricanes Ian and Nicole.

Forecasters and researchers relied on this invaluable data coupled with NOAA’s advanced geostationary and polar-orbiting weather satellites, NOAA's weather buoys and other sources before, during and after storms throughout this destructive hurricane season.

While the 2022 season is drawing to a close, now is not the time to let your guard down. The 2023 hurricane season will officially begin on June 1. Let’s take the time to ensure your family is Weather-Ready for the season ahead. NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center, a division of the National Weather Service, will issue its initial 2023 seasonal outlook in May.

There is much to be done as we prepare for the 2023 Hurricane Season, identifying stay-back personnel (Fort Stewart-Hunter Army Airfield numbers still remains high); two Force Protection Exercises for Garrison and 3rd Infantry Division to plan; a Hurricane Plan Review; and command post exercises with a new system to replace WebEOC to be learned by all Fort Stewart-Hunter Army Airfield garrison Emergency Operation Center members.

It's never too early to start looking over your family plans now for the 2023 Hurricane Season.

(U.S. Army Story by Mack McPherson, Installation Emergency Manager)

The **2022 Atlantic hurricane season** was a near-average yet destructive [Atlantic hurricane season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_hurricane_season "Atlantic hurricane season"). Despite having an average number of [named storms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclone_naming "Tropical cyclone naming") and a below average amount of major hurricanes,[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-3) it became the fourth-costliest Atlantic hurricane season on record, behind only [2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2024 Atlantic hurricane season"), [2005](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2005 Atlantic hurricane season"), and [2017](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2017 Atlantic hurricane season"), mostly due to [Hurricane Ian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Ian "Hurricane Ian"). The season officially began on June 1, and ended on November 30. These dates, adopted by convention, historically describe the period in each year when most [subtropical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtropical_cyclone "Subtropical cyclone") or [tropical cyclogenesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclogenesis "Tropical cyclogenesis") occurs in the Atlantic Ocean.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-4) This year's first Atlantic named storm, [Tropical Storm Alex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Alex_(2022) "Tropical Storm Alex (2022)"), developed four days after the start of the season, making this the first season since [2014](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2014 Atlantic hurricane season") not to have a pre-season named storm.

Two systems developed on July 1. [Tropical Storm Bonnie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Bonnie_(2022) "Hurricane Bonnie (2022)") formed and made landfall near the [Costa Rica–Nicaragua border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica%E2%80%93Nicaragua_border "Costa Rica–Nicaragua border"). It then crossed over into the [Pacific basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Pacific_hurricane_season "2022 Pacific hurricane season"), becoming the first to survive the crossover from the Atlantic to the Pacific since [Hurricane Otto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Otto "Hurricane Otto") in [2016](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2016 Atlantic hurricane season"). Also, Tropical Storm Colin formed abruptly and made landfall in [South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina "South Carolina"), before quickly weakening and dissipating the next day. Following this activity, tropical cyclogenesis was suppressed across the basin for several weeks by a combination of increased [wind shear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_shear "Wind shear") and the presence of the [Saharan Air Layer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saharan_Air_Layer "Saharan Air Layer"). This stopped all tropical cyclogenesis in August, the first season to do so since [1997](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Atlantic_hurricane_season "1997 Atlantic hurricane season"), and the first during a [La Niña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Ni%C3%B1a "La Niña"). This pause in activity lasted sixty days, ending when hurricanes Danielle and [Earl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Earl_(2022) "Hurricane Earl (2022)") formed on September 1 and 3 respectively. Danielle become the season's first hurricane; the last season to have its first hurricane develop this late was [2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2013 Atlantic hurricane season").

Activity then increased tremendously towards the end of September as four named storms formed in quick succession. Among them, [Hurricane Fiona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Fiona "Hurricane Fiona") became the season's first major hurricane on September 20, which is about three weeks later than when the first one typically forms.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-EOTS_092022-5) As an extratropical cyclone it became the strongest storm in Canadian history, as measured by [atmospheric pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_pressure "Atmospheric pressure"), and caused significant damage in [Atlantic Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Canada "Atlantic Canada"). Hurricane Ian then became the second major hurricane of the season on September 27 and the only Category 5 of the season on September 28 and inflicted an estimated $113.1 billion in damage to western [Cuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuba "Cuba"), [Southwestern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwest_Florida "Southwest Florida") and [Central Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Florida "Central Florida"), and the [Carolinas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolinas "Carolinas"). [Hurricane Julia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Julia_(2022) "Hurricane Julia (2022)") formed in early October and became the second storm of the season to cross over into the Pacific basin intact after traversing Nicaragua, making this season the first to have more than one crossover system since [1996](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Atlantic_hurricane_season "1996 Atlantic hurricane season"). The last storm in the season, [Hurricane Nicole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Nicole_(2022) "Hurricane Nicole (2022)"), made landfall on the coasts of the Bahamas and Florida. It was the first November hurricane to make landfall in Florida since [Kate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Kate_(1985) "Hurricane Kate (1985)") in [1985](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1985_Atlantic_hurricane_season "1985 Atlantic hurricane season"), and caused about $1 billion in damage in areas devastated by Ian six weeks earlier. Tropical cyclones during this season collectively caused at least 304 deaths and more than $117.7 billion in damage, making it one of the costliest seasons on record.

Most forecasting agencies anticipated a well-above average season due to warmer-than-normal [sea surface temperatures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_surface_temperature "Sea surface temperature") and a favorable [El Niño–Southern Oscillation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Ni%C3%B1o%E2%80%93Southern_Oscillation "El Niño–Southern Oscillation") pattern, limiting the chances of [El Niño](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Ni%C3%B1o "El Niño") developing. While conducive conditions such as warmer sea surface temperatures and a La Niña came to fruition, the unfavorable wind shear pattern with drier air and Saharan Air Layer suppressed tropical cyclogenesis through most of July and the entirety of August, with the latter typically being among the most active climatologically.

In advance of, and during, each hurricane season, several [forecasts of hurricane activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclone_seasonal_forecasting "Tropical cyclone seasonal forecasting") are issued by national meteorological services, scientific agencies, and noted hurricane experts. These include forecasters from the United States [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Oceanic_and_Atmospheric_Administration "National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration") (NOAA)'s [Climate Prediction Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_Prediction_Center "Climate Prediction Center"), Tropical Storm Risk (TSR), the United Kingdom's [Met Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Met_Office "Met Office") (UKMO), and Philip J. Klotzbach and their associates at [Colorado State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_University "Colorado State University") (CSU). The forecasts include weekly and monthly changes in significant factors that help determine the number of tropical storms, hurricanes, and major hurricanes within a particular year. According to NOAA and CSU, the average [Atlantic hurricane season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_hurricane_season "Atlantic hurricane season") between 1991 and 2020 contained roughly 14 tropical storms, seven hurricanes, three major hurricanes, and an [accumulated cyclone energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accumulated_cyclone_energy "Accumulated cyclone energy") (ACE) index of 74–126 units.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Dec21TSR-27) Broadly speaking, ACE is a measure of the power of a tropical or subtropical storm multiplied by the length of time it existed. It is only calculated for full advisories on specific tropical and subtropical systems reaching or exceeding wind speeds of 39 mph (63 km/h).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Background-6) NOAA typically categorizes a season as above-average, average, or below-average based on the cumulative ACE index, but the number of tropical storms, hurricanes, and major hurricanes within a hurricane season is sometimes also considered.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Background-6)

### Pre-season forecasts

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Pre-season forecasts")]

On December 9, 2021, CSU issued an extended-range forecast for the 2022 hurricane season, giving a 40% chance of near-average activity with 13–16 named storms, 6–8 hurricanes, 2–3 major hurricanes, and an ACE index of about 130 units. The forecast also gave a 25% chance that the ACE Index would end up being around 170 units, and a 25% likelihood the likelihood that the index would end up around 80.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Dec21CSU-8) TSR also issued an extended-range forecast on December 10, 2021.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Dec22TSR-9) It predicted overall near-average tropical activity with its ACE index, anticipating 18 tropical storms, 8 hurricanes, and 3 intense hurricanes to form during the season. One of their factors was the expectation of a neutral [El Niño-Southern Oscillation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Ni%C3%B1o-Southern_Oscillation "El Niño-Southern Oscillation") condition by the third quarter of 2022. This outlook had "large uncertainties".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Dec22TSR-9)

In their April 6, 2022, forecast, TSR's number of named storms remained unchanged, while they slightly increased the number of major hurricane from three to four.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Apr6TSR-10) On the following day, CSU issued their first extended-range seasonal forecast for the 2022 Atlantic hurricane season, predicting well-above-average activity, with 19 named storms, 9 hurricanes, 4 major hurricanes, and an ACE index of 160 units. Their factors supporting an active hurricane season included above average-sea surface temperatures in the subtropical Atlantic Ocean and Caribbean Sea, and a cool neutral ENSO or weak La Niña pattern, corresponding to a low chance of an [El Niño](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Ni%C3%B1o "El Niño").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Apr7CSU-11)[The Weather Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Weather_Channel "The Weather Channel") (TWC) issued their first seasonal forecast on April 14, calling for 20 named storms, 8 hurricanes, and 4 major hurricanes.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Apr14TWC-12) On the same day, the [University of Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Arizona "University of Arizona") (UA) issued its seasonal prediction for a slightly above-average hurricane season, with 14 named storms, 7 hurricanes, 3 major hurricanes, and an ACE index of 129 units.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Apr14UA-13)[North Carolina State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina_State_University "North Carolina State University") (NCSU) made its prediction for the season on April 20, calling for an above-average season with 17 to 21 named storms, 7 to 9 hurricanes, and 3 to 5 major hurricanes.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Apr20NCSU-14)

On May 9, [Pennsylvania State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_State_University "Pennsylvania State University") predicted 14.9 +/- 3.8 tropical storms, or a range of 11 to 19 named storms.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-pennstate-15) On May 23, UKMO issued their own forecast for the 2022 season, predicting an above-average season with 18 named storms, 9 hurricanes, and 4 major hurricanes, with a 70% chance that each of these statistics will fall between 13 and 23, 6 and 12, and 2 and 6, respectively.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-May23UKMO-16) The following day, NOAA's Climate Prediction Center issued their forecasts for the season, predicting a 65% chance of above-average activity and 25% chance for below-average activity, with 14–21 named storms, 6–10 hurricanes, and 3–6 major hurricanes.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-May24NOAA-17) TSR released another prediction on May 31 that was unchanged from its April 6 forecast: 18 named storms, 8 hurricanes, and 4 major hurricanes.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-May31TSR-18)

### Mid-season forecasts

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mid-season forecasts")]

On June 2, CSU updated their extended-range seasonal forecast, increasing the amount of tropical cyclones to 20 named storms, 10 hurricanes, 5 major hurricanes, and an overall ACE index of 180 units. This was done after a later analysis of the lower chances of an El Niño during the season, as well as a warmer-than-average tropical Atlantic.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Jun2CSU-19) TWC's second outlook, released on June 17, slightly increased the number of named storms to 21 and hurricanes to 9, but left the number of major hurricanes at 4.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Jun17TWC-20) On June 20, 2022, UA updated its seasonal prediction, which is very similar to its April prediction, with 15 named storms, 7 hurricanes, 3 major hurricanes, and an ACE index of 131 units.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Jun20UA-21) On July 5, TSR released their third forecast for the season, slightly increasing their numbers to 18 named storms, 9 hurricanes, and 4 major hurricanes. This prediction was largely based on the persistence of the weak La Niña into the third quarter of the year.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Jul5TSR-22) On July 7, CSU did not make changes to their updated prediction of 20 named storms, 10 hurricanes, and 5 major hurricanes.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Jul7CSU-23) UKMO's updated forecast on August 2 called for 16 named storms, 6 hurricanes, and 4 major hurricanes.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Aug2UKMO-24) Two days later, NOAA and CSU each revised their activity outlook slightly downward, though both still predicted that the season would end up being busier than the 30-year average. The revisions were made in part because of the relative slow start to the season (as compared to the past few years), with only three short-lived named storms as of the start of August.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-EOTS8422-25) The third and final TWC seasonal forecast, issued on August 18, decreased the number of named storms to 17, hurricanes to 7, and major hurricanes to 3.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Aug18TWC-26)

### Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Background")]

[![Image 7: A satellite photo of Tropical Storm Earl (bottom left) and Hurricane Danielle (top right) both active simultaneously on September 5, 2022.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/Danielle_and_Earl_on_September_5_2022.jpg/250px-Danielle_and_Earl_on_September_5_2022.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Danielle_and_Earl_on_September_5_2022.jpg)

[Tropical Storm Earl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Earl_(2022) "Hurricane Earl (2022)") (bottom left) and Hurricane Danielle (top right) on September 5

Officially, the 2022 Atlantic hurricane season ran from June 1 to November 30.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-pennstate-15) A total of 16 tropical cyclones developed, 14 of which intensified into named storms. Of those, eight strengthened into a hurricane, while two systems reached major hurricane intensity. Thus, the season was near-average compared to NOAA's 1991–2020 mean of 14 named storms, 7 hurricanes, and 3 major hurricanes.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-TWSAT_1122-2) The near-average number of named storms ended the record six-year streak of above-average activity in the Atlantic.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-bizarre-28) A strong La Niña and slightly above-normal West African Monsoon season led to the mostly average activity. However, intense wind shear and the suppression of moisture in the atmosphere by the [Saharan Air Layer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saharan_Air_Layer "Saharan Air Layer") led to an unusual mid-season cessation in tropical cyclogenesis that lasted nearly two months,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-noaa_11/29-29)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-30) with no named storms in the Atlantic between July 3 and August 31 for the first time since [1941](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1941_Atlantic_hurricane_season "1941 Atlantic hurricane season").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-bizarre-28)

Hurricanes [Fiona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Fiona "Hurricane Fiona") and [Ian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Ian "Hurricane Ian") inflicted historically significant impacts on certain areas. After Fiona caused a few billion dollars in damage in Puerto Rico, its remnants struck [Nova Scotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nova_Scotia "Nova Scotia") as a powerful [extratropical cyclone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extratropical_cyclone "Extratropical cyclone"), becoming the costliest weather disaster on record in [Atlantic Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Canada "Atlantic Canada").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Fiona_TCR-31) Ian became both the costliest Florida hurricane and the third-costliest on record in the United States, behind only [Hurricane Katrina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Katrina "Hurricane Katrina") in [2005](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2005 Atlantic hurricane season") and [Hurricane Harvey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Harvey "Hurricane Harvey") in [2017](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2017 Atlantic hurricane season"). Additionally, 150 fatalities occurred in Florida,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-:1-32) making Ian the deadliest tropical cyclone in the state since the [1935 Labor Day hurricane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1935_Labor_Day_hurricane "1935 Labor Day hurricane").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-bizarre-28) Collectively, the tropical cyclones of the 2022 Atlantic hurricane season caused at least 304 fatalities and more than $117.708 billion in damage,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-atcr-33) making it one of the costliest seasons of all time.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-EOTS_1110-34)

This season's [ACE index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accumulated_cyclone_energy "Accumulated cyclone energy") was approximately 94.6 units,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-35) which was 77% of the long-term (30-year) average of 123.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-TWSAT_1122-2) This was the first season since [2007](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2007 Atlantic hurricane season") to have an ACE value that is near-average. All seasons from 2008 to 2021 were either below or above-average.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Apr7CSU-11)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9c/Fiona%2C_Gaston%2C_Hermine_and_09L_on_September_23%2C_2022.png/250px-Fiona%2C_Gaston%2C_Hermine_and_09L_on_September_23%2C_2022.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fiona,_Gaston,_Hermine_and_09L_on_September_23,_2022.png)

Four tropical cyclones active simultaneously on September 23: [Hurricane Fiona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Fiona "Hurricane Fiona") (top-left), Tropical Storm Gaston (top-right), [Tropical Storm Hermine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Hermine_(2022) "Tropical Storm Hermine (2022)") (bottom-right), and Tropical Depression Nine (bottom-left, which ultimately became [Hurricane Ian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Ian "Hurricane Ian")). The wave that would later spawn Tropical Depression Eleven can be seen to the left of Hermine.

Overall, [NOAA Hurricane Hunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NOAA_Hurricane_Hunters "NOAA Hurricane Hunters") logged more than 582 flight hours while conducting 65 eyewall passages and deploying more than 1,700 scientific instruments, including [dropsondes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropsonde "Dropsonde"). Additionally, the Gulfstream IV-SP took off from the Cabo Verde Islands in August, becoming the easternmost hurricane hunter flight. NOAA also launched an [Altius-600](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altius-600 "Altius-600") for the first time, which recorded wind speed data on Hurricane Ian as it approached landfall in Florida. Crews of flights conducted by the [National Ocean Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Ocean_Service "National Ocean Service") took thousands of aerial images of the destruction caused by Ian, which especially assisted with identifying pollutants and areas requiring extensive [marine debris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_debris "Marine debris") cleanup. NOAA's King Air and Twin Otter aircraft were also involved in a similar mission in the aftermath of Ian and Hurricane Nicole, logging more than 41 flight hours.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-noaa_11/29-29)

### Early season activity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Early season activity")]

The 2022 season was the first since [2014](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2014 Atlantic hurricane season") to not have a pre-season named storm. Activity began with the formation of [Tropical Storm Alex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Alex_(2022) "Tropical Storm Alex (2022)") on June 5, after several days of slow development while traversing the [Gulf of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Mexico "Gulf of Mexico") and then moving over Central Florida.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-36) The storm peaked at near-hurricane strength before becoming extratropical on the following day over the Central North Atlantic. On July 1, [Tropical Storm Bonnie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Bonnie_(2022) "Hurricane Bonnie (2022)") formed in the Southern [Caribbean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean_Sea "Caribbean Sea") and made landfall shortly thereafter near the Costa Rica–Nicaragua border. It then [crossed over](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Atlantic%E2%80%93Pacific_crossover_hurricanes "List of Atlantic–Pacific crossover hurricanes") into the Pacific basin a day later, the first storm to do so since [Hurricane Otto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Otto "Hurricane Otto") in [2016](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2016 Atlantic hurricane season"),[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-37) where it would become a Category 3 hurricane.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-btcr-38) Also on July 1, a low-pressure system off the U.S. Atlantic coast near [Savannah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savannah,_Georgia "Savannah, Georgia"), [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)"), abruptly organized into Tropical Storm Colin, a short-lived storm that dissipated the next day inland over northeastern South Carolina.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Colin_TCR-39) Tropical cyclogenesis then ceased for almost two months, with 2022 becoming the first season since [1997](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Atlantic_hurricane_season "1997 Atlantic hurricane season") in which no tropical cyclones formed in August.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-EOTS_83122-40) A disturbance over the Gulf of Mexico was briefly designated as a _potential tropical cyclone_ during the month, but it did not organize into a tropical cyclone before moving inland over Northeastern [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-PTC4TCR-41)

Tropical activity ultimately resumed with the formation of Tropical Storm Danielle over the central Atlantic on September 1. The storm intensified into a hurricane the following day, the latest first hurricane since [2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2013 Atlantic hurricane season").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-42) It remained nearly stationary far to the west of the [Azores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azores "Azores") for several days before moving northeastward and becoming extratropical on September 8 without affecting any land areas.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-dtcr-43) Additionally, a slow-developing disturbance east of the [Lesser Antilles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lesser_Antilles "Lesser Antilles") became organized and developed into Tropical Storm Earl late on September 2. It strengthened into a hurricane, tracked east of [Bermuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bermuda "Bermuda"), fluctuating between Category 1 and 2 intensity, and then became extratropical near [Newfoundland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newfoundland_(island) "Newfoundland (island)") on September 10.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-etcr-44) Four days later, Tropical Storm Fiona formed in the Central Atlantic. Fiona eventually became a hurricane, striking both [Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Rico "Puerto Rico") and the [Dominican Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominican_Republic "Dominican Republic") before becoming the season's first major hurricane as it passed by the [Turks and Caicos Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turks_and_Caicos_Islands "Turks and Caicos Islands") on September 20. That same day, Tropical Storm Gaston formed over the Central Atlantic and moved through the Western Azores. Fiona strengthened into a Category 4 hurricane as it passed west of Bermuda and transitioned into a powerful extratropical cyclone on September 23, just before striking Nova Scotia.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Fiona_TCR-31) That same day, Tropical Depression Nine formed in the Caribbean Sea and Tropical Depression Ten formed in the eastern tropical Atlantic, marking the first time since [2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2020 Atlantic hurricane season") that four tropical cyclones were active simultaneously in the Atlantic basin.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-YCC_092422-45)

Tropical Depression Nine became [Hurricane Ian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Ian "Hurricane Ian"), the deadliest and most destructive storm of the season. Ian made landfall in western Cuba and crossed the [Florida Keys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Keys "Florida Keys") as a Category 3 hurricane, before briefly becoming a Category 5 hurricane. It then made landfall in southwestern Florida as a high-end Category 4 hurricane, with winds of 150 mph (240 km/h), the strongest storm to hit the area in terms of windspeed. The storm later made landfall in South Carolina as a Category 1.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-:1-32) Tropical Depression Ten attained tropical storm strength first, becoming [Tropical Storm Hermine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Hermine_(2022) "Tropical Storm Hermine (2022)").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Hermine_TCR-46) It was one of the easternmost Atlantic tropical storms on record,[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-YCC_92222-47) and brought heavy rainfall to the [Canary Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands "Canary Islands").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Hermine_TCR-46) Next, Tropical Depression Eleven formed during the last week in September, and then Tropical Depression Twelve formed one week later. Ultimately, neither cyclone strengthened into a tropical storm.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-11tcr-48)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-12tcr-49) Soon thereafter, [Hurricane Julia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Julia_(2022) "Hurricane Julia (2022)") formed just off the coast of [Venezuela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venezuela "Venezuela") on October 7. After traversing Nicaragua intact, Julia entered the Pacific basin.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-jtcr-50) Not since [1996](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Atlantic_hurricane_season "1996 Atlantic hurricane season") has more than one storm crossed between the Atlantic and Pacific basins intact during a single season.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Henson_EOTS-51) On October 11, Tropical Storm Karl formed in the [Bay of Campeche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_of_Campeche "Bay of Campeche"), moved erratically over open waters, before degenerating into a remnant low offshore of Mexico three days later.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Karl_TCR-52) Hurricane Martin was the second largest Atlantic hurricane on record as measured by diameter, behind only [Hurricane Sandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Sandy "Hurricane Sandy"), with tropical-storm-force winds spanning 1,040 miles (1,670 km).[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-53)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-54) Martin and [Lisa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Lisa_(2022) "Hurricane Lisa (2022)") were both at hurricane strength on November 2, thus, for the first time since [Michelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Michelle "Hurricane Michelle") and [Noel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Noel_(2001) "Hurricane Noel (2001)") in November.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-55) Soon thereafter, Hurricane Nicole formed on November 7, also tying 2001 for the most hurricanes in November, with three.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-bizarre-28) Nicole impacted the [Greater Antilles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Antilles "Greater Antilles"), the [Bahamas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahamas "Bahamas"), and the [Eastern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_United_States "Eastern United States"), becoming the ### Tropical Storm Alex

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Tropical Storm Alex")]

Tropical storm(SSHWS)
[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/Alex_2022-06-05_2210Z.png/250px-Alex_2022-06-05_2210Z.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alex_2022-06-05_2210Z.png)[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e8/Alex_2022_path.png/250px-Alex_2022_path.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alex_2022_path.png)
Duration June 5– June 6
Peak intensity 70 mph (110 km/h) (1-min);  
984[mbar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_(unit) "Bar (unit)")([hPa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pascal_(unit) "Pascal (unit)"))

Main article: [Tropical Storm Alex (2022)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Alex_(2022) "Tropical Storm Alex (2022)")

In late May, the mid-level remnants of [Hurricane Agatha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Agatha "Hurricane Agatha") in the Pacific basin interacted with a Central American Gyre. Consequently, a gradual increase in deep [convection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_convection "Atmospheric convection") occurred over the [Yucatán Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yucat%C3%A1n_Peninsula "Yucatán Peninsula") and the northwestern Caribbean Sea, which led to the development of a [low-pressure area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low-pressure_area "Low-pressure area") just north of the [Belize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belize "Belize")-Mexico border on June 2. After emerging into the southeastern Gulf of Mexico early the next day, the disturbance made multiple attempts at organizing into a tropical cyclone and attained tropical storm-force winds. However, strong [wind shear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_shear "Wind shear") kept the system disorganized before it struck [Southwest Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwest_Florida "Southwest Florida") on June 4. Several hours later, the disturbance emerged into the Atlantic, where it developed into Tropical Storm Alex at 00:00[UTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time "Coordinated Universal Time") on June 5 about 85 mi (135 km) north of [Grand Bahama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Bahama "Grand Bahama"). Additional intensification occurred as Alex moved east-northeastward due to mid-latitude westerly flow, reaching sustained winds of 70 mph (110 km/h) around 18:00 UTC. However, drier air caused Alex to weaken on the following day, with the storm transitioning into an extratropical cyclone at 12:00 UTC roughly 105 mi (170 km) north-northwest of Bermuda. The remnants of Alex were absorbed by a baroclinic zone early on June 7.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-atcr-33)

Due to the threat the developing system posed to [Cuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuba "Cuba"), the [Florida Keys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Keys "Florida Keys"), and [South Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Florida "South Florida"), the [National Hurricane Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Hurricane_Center "National Hurricane Center") initiated advisories on it, designating it as _[Potential Tropical Cyclone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary\_of\_tropical\_cyclone\_terms#P "Glossary of tropical cyclone terms") One_. The precursor to Alex dropped heavy precipitation in these regions.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-atcr-33) During a 30-hour period on June 2–3, Paso Real de San Diego in the province of [Pinar del Río](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinar_del_R%C3%ADo_Province "Pinar del Río Province") recorded about 12 inches (301 mm) of rain, and [Playa Girón](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playa_Gir%C3%B3n "Playa Girón") in [Matanzas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matanzas_Province "Matanzas Province") received over 8 inches (193 mm).[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-57) There were four storm-related deaths in Cuba, while about 750 homes, 7,900 [acres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acre "Acre") (3,200[ha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hectare "Hectare")) of crops,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-atcr-33) and numerous bridges suffered flood damage.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-58) According to AON, damages from flooding totaled at least US$25 million in Cuba.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-:2-59) In Florida, several locations in the Upper Keys and the [Miami metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_metropolitan_area "Miami metropolitan area") observed between 10 and 15 in (250 and 380 mm) of rainfall, with a peak total of 15.28 in (388 mm) near [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood,_Florida "Hollywood, Florida"). Extensive street flooding occurred in the Miami area, but water entered only a few properties. Across [Broward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broward_County,_Florida "Broward County, Florida") and [Miami-Dade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami-Dade_County,_Florida "Miami-Dade County, Florida") counties combined, there were about 3,500 power outages.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-atcr-33) Damage from the precursor to Alex in Florida totaled $104,000.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-NCDCAlex-60) However, it was later determined that flood damages in Florida were more than $350 million.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-:2-59)

### Tropical Storm Bonnie

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Tropical Storm Bonnie")]
