Hurricane Idalia's wind history.

### United States

On August 31, 2023, President Joe Biden said that he had spoken to Florida Governor Ron DeSantis and other governors about Idalia and that he had approved of their requests for disaster and emergency declarations.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-119)

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/P20230902OC-1140_%2853234993953%29.jpg/250px-P20230902OC-1140_%2853234993953%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:P20230902OC-1140_(53234993953).jpg)

President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") addressing the impacts of the storm in [Live Oak, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_Oak,_Florida "Live Oak, Florida")

#### Florida

On August 30, Governor Ron DeSantis visited Perry and gave a press conference update on the state's response to the storm, where he spoke alongside several state and local officials.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-120) President Biden announced that he had directed FEMA Administrator [Deanne Criswell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deanne_Criswell "Deanne Criswell") to fly to Florida and meet with DeSantis and that up to 1,500 federal personnel as well as 900 members of the [Coast Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Coast_Guard "United States Coast Guard") were being sent to respond to the hurricane's impacts.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-121)[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-122)

On September 2, President Biden, First Lady [Jill Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jill_Biden "Jill Biden"), and FEMA Administrator Deanne Criswell, landed at [Gainesville Regional Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gainesville_Regional_Airport "Gainesville Regional Airport") before embarking on an aerial tour of affected areas within the state. Biden then visited Suwannee Pineview Elementary School in [Live Oak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_Oak,_Florida "Live Oak, Florida") where he was briefed on the damage caused by the storm. Biden met with residents of Live Oak as well as Live Oak Mayor Frank Davis and Senator [Rick Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Scott "Rick Scott") among other officials.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-123)

FEMA opened up six temporary Disaster and Recovery Centers across Dixie, [Levy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levy_County,_Florida "Levy County, Florida"), [Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton_County,_Florida "Hamilton County, Florida"), [Suwannee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suwannee_County,_Florida "Suwannee County, Florida"), [Madison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_County,_Florida "Madison County, Florida"), and [Lafayette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lafayette_County,_Florida "Lafayette County, Florida") counties.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-124) Fourteen counties; [Citrus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citrus_County,_Florida "Citrus County, Florida"), [Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_County,_Florida "Columbia County, Florida"), Dixie, [Gilchrist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilchrist_County,_Florida "Gilchrist County, Florida"), Hamilton, [Hernando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hernando_County,_Florida "Hernando County, Florida"), [Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_County,_Florida "Jefferson County, Florida"), Lafayette, Levy, Madison, Pasco, Pinellas, Suwannee, and [Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_County,_Florida "Taylor County, Florida"), were made eligible for Individual, Critical Needs, Clean and Sanitize, and Disaster Unemployment Assistance.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-125)

The [Small Business Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small_Business_Administration "Small Business Administration") made available Business Physical Disaster, Economic Injury Disaster, and Home Disaster loans available to Citrus, Columbia, Dixie, Gilchrist, Hamilton, Hernando, Jefferson, Lafayette, Levy, Madison, Pasco, Pinellas, Suwannee, and Taylor counties. Meanwhile, Alachua, [Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baker_County,_Florida "Baker County, Florida"), [Hillsborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillsborough_County,_Florida "Hillsborough County, Florida"), [Leon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leon_County,_Florida "Leon County, Florida"), [Marion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marion_County,_Florida "Marion County, Florida"), [Polk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polk_County,_Florida "Polk County, Florida"), [Sumter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sumter_County,_Florida "Sumter County, Florida"), [Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_County,_Florida "Union County, Florida"), and [Wakulla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wakulla_County,_Florida "Wakulla County, Florida") counties were only eligible for Economic Injury Disaster loans.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-126)

The hurricane began an apparent American Flamingo population boom within the state, as wildlife experts believe many of the birds that were brought from the Caribbean and Yucatán Peninsula into the United States by Idalia's winds did not leave the state like they did in other parts of the country and instead settled down. While flamingos are native to South Florida, they have not existed in significant numbers since the 19th century, when hunting drove them out of the state, but according to [Audubon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audubon "Audubon") who conducted a census on the flamingo population in February, finding 101 birds, they have a chance to reassert themselves in Florida.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-127)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-128)[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-129)

#### Georgia

On September 1, Governor Brian Kemp toured Valdosta with Georgia First Lady [Marty Kemp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Kemp "Marty Kemp") and other state officials to survey damage from Idalia. While in Valdosta, [Georgia Emergency Management and Homeland Security Agency Director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Emergency_Management_and_Homeland_Security_Agency "Georgia Emergency Management and Homeland Security Agency") Chris Stallings announced that the state had requested federal assistance from FEMA for the clean-up efforts within the state.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:10-97)

The SBA declared [Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cook_County,_Georgia "Cook County, Georgia"), [Glynn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glynn_County,_Georgia "Glynn County, Georgia"), and [Lowndes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowndes_County,_Georgia "Lowndes County, Georgia") counties eligible for Physical and Economic Injury Disaster Loans due being approved federal disaster relief funds from FEMA due to President Biden approving a major disaster declaration for the counties, which also made those counties eligible for Individual and Public Assistance from FEMA.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-130)[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-131) Meanwhile, [Berrien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berrien_County,_Georgia "Berrien County, Georgia"), [Brooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooks_County,_Georgia "Brooks County, Georgia"), [Camden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camden_County,_Georgia "Camden County, Georgia"), [Colquitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colquitt_County,_Georgia "Colquitt County, Georgia"), [Echols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Echols_County,_Georgia "Echols County, Georgia"), [Lanier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lanier_County,_Georgia "Lanier County, Georgia"), [McIntosh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McIntosh_County,_Georgia "McIntosh County, Georgia"), [Tift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tift_County,_Georgia "Tift County, Georgia"), and [Wayne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_County,_Georgia "Wayne County, Georgia") counties were made eligible to apply only for Economic Injury Disaster Loans.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-132) The [United States Department of Agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Agriculture "United States Department of Agriculture") has also approved of financial aid to farmers in Berrien County with crop damage.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-133)

Part of the **[2023 Atlantic hurricane season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2023 Atlantic hurricane season")**

**Hurricane Idalia** was a powerful and destructive [tropical cyclone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclone "Tropical cyclone") that caused significant damage across parts of the [southeastern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_United_States "Southeastern United States"), especially [North Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Florida "North Florida"), in late August 2023. The ninth [named storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclone_naming "Tropical cyclone naming"),[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-3) third hurricane, and second major hurricane of the [2023 Atlantic hurricane season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2023 Atlantic hurricane season"), Idalia formed from a low-pressure area that crossed [Central America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_America "Central America") from the eastern [Pacific Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Ocean "Pacific Ocean"). Gradual development ensued as it meandered in the western part of the [Caribbean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean_Sea "Caribbean Sea"); the system was upgraded to a tropical depression on August 26, 2023, and strengthened into a tropical storm a day later, receiving the name _Idalia_. It traversed the [Gulf of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Mexico "Gulf of Mexico") where it underwent [rapid intensification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapid_intensification "Rapid intensification"), briefly becoming a [Category 4 hurricane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category_4_hurricane "Category 4 hurricane") before weakening and making landfall in the [Big Bend region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Bend_(Florida) "Big Bend (Florida)") of [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida") as a low-end Category 3 hurricane on August 30. Idalia remained a hurricane as it moved through Northern Florida and crossed into [Southeast Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Georgia "Southeast Georgia"); it then pushed into the [Carolinas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolinas "Carolinas") as a tropical storm. On August 31, Idalia emerged into the Atlantic, where it transitioned into a post-tropical cyclone that same day. Later, it passed south of [Bermuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bermuda "Bermuda"), made a counterclockwise loop, then meandered off the coast of [Nova Scotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nova_Scotia "Nova Scotia") while winding down.

Idalia caused significant damage to thousands of homes, businesses, and other infrastructure along its inland path, primarily in Florida, where winds and the resulting floodwaters were highest. Its [storm surge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_surge "Storm surge") was record-breaking from the Big Bend region south to [Tampa Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tampa_Bay "Tampa Bay"). In Tampa Bay roads were flooded over, and high waters submerged hundreds of cars. The system also spawned a [tornado outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak "Tornado outbreak") with around 12 confirmed tornadoes. Idalia was the most powerful hurricane to hit Florida's Big Bend region since [Hurricane Easy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Easy_(1950) "Hurricane Easy (1950)") in 1950.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-TCR-1) Five people died in storm-related incidents in the two states. The [NCEI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCEI "NCEI") estimates that Hurricane Idalia was responsible for $3.5 billion in damages. The hurricane's remnants produced dangerous rip currents across the Eastern United States during [Labor Day Weekend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labor_Day_Weekend "Labor Day Weekend"), resulting in several additional deaths and numerous rescues.

On August 24, 2023, a [trough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trough_(meteorology) "Trough (meteorology)") of low pressure formed in the Eastern Pacific basin offshore of the Central America coast.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-5) The disturbance crossed over into the Atlantic basin the following day, and began to organize as it moved northward through the western [Caribbean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean_Sea "Caribbean Sea"). The pace of organization quickened on August 26, while the disturbance was located near the northeastern [Yucatán Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yucat%C3%A1n_Peninsula "Yucatán Peninsula"), and at 21:00 UTC it was upgraded to Tropical Depression Ten.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-6) Later that day, and into the next, the depression drifted due to weak surrounding steering currents, with its center moving in a small counterclockwise loop.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-7)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-8) The depression became Tropical Storm Idalia at 15:15 UTC on August 27, after a [NOAA Hurricane Hunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NOAA_Hurricane_Hunters "NOAA Hurricane Hunters") flight reported that the storm's winds had increased to 40 mph (65 km/h).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-9) Early the next morning, Idalia began moving northward[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-10) toward the [Yucatán Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yucat%C3%A1n_Channel "Yucatán Channel") west of [Cuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuba "Cuba"), intensifying along the way despite being impacted by moderate northwesterly wind shear.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-EOTS_warnings-11)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/35/Idalia_peak_and_landfall.gif/250px-Idalia_peak_and_landfall.gif?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Idalia_peak_and_landfall.gif)

Idalia attaining Category 4 intensity and making landfall early on August 30

By 09:00 UTC on August 29, after passing near the [western tip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_San_Antonio,_Cuba "Cape San Antonio, Cuba") of Cuba, Idalia had developed an inner core and almost complete eyewall and the NHC upgraded the storm to a [Category 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saffir%E2%80%93Simpson_scale "Saffir–Simpson scale") hurricane.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-12) Later that day, Idalia began to rapidly intensify, reaching Category 2 strength[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-13) as it benefited from exceptional conditions, with [sea-surface temperatures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea-surface_temperatures "Sea-surface temperatures") of 88°F (31°C), generally low [wind shear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_shear "Wind shear"), and high [relative humidity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relative_humidity "Relative humidity") levels.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-EOTS_1708-14) Idalia continued to rapidly intensify as it accelerated northward off the [Florida Suncoast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Suncoast "Florida Suncoast") and approached the [Big Bend region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Bend_(Florida) "Big Bend (Florida)"), reaching its peak intensity of Category 4 strength on the morning of August 30, a few hours prior to [landfall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landfall "Landfall"), with maximum sustained winds of 130 mph (215 km/h) and a minimum central pressure of 942 mbar (27.82 inHg).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-TCR-1) This marked a wind increase of 55 mph (89 km/h) during the 24 hour period ending at 09:00 UTC on August 30, making it one of fastest rates of tropical cyclone intensification ever observed in the Atlantic basin 24 hours before landfall. At its peak, the NHC described the system as having "a small eye surrounded by very cold clouds tops, especially in the western quadrant".[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-15) Idalia's intensification was then halted by an [eyewall replacement cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eyewall_replacement_cycle "Eyewall replacement cycle"), which caused it to weaken prior to landfall.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-EOTS_3008-16) Idalia made landfall at 11:45 UTC, about 20 miles (30 km) south of [Perry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perry,_Florida "Perry, Florida"), Florida, as a Category 3 hurricane, with sustained winds of 115 mph (185 km/h) and a minimum central pressure of 950 mbar (28.05 inHg).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-TCR-1)

The system quickly weakened inland as it pushed through [North Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Florida "North Florida"), becoming a tropical storm later that day after crossing into [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-Forbes_3008-17)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-18) Strong southwesterly wind shear then pushed the storm's convection well north and east of its center as it moved off the northeastern [South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina "South Carolina") coast and emerged into the Atlantic Ocean on the morning of August 31.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-19) That afternoon, Idalia transitioned into a post-tropical cyclone about 65 miles (105 km) southeast of [Cape Hatteras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Hatteras "Cape Hatteras"), [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina "North Carolina").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-Advisory_#21-20) As the storm moved to the east-southeast the following day, light wind shear along its path enabled the system to maintain its structure and intensity despite the lack of convection.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-21) The storm impacted [Bermuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bermuda "Bermuda") with tropical-storm-force winds on September 2, as it passed just to the south. Idalia's remnant low then absorbed [Tropical Storm Gert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Gert_(2023) "Tropical Storm Gert (2023)") on September 4[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-22) and lingered off the coast of [Atlantic Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Canada "Atlantic Canada") for several days, before dissipating on September 8.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-23)

## Preparations

### Cuba

More than 10,000 people were evacuated from [Pinar del Río](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinar_del_R%C3%ADo_Province "Pinar del Río Province") and [Artemisa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemisa_Province "Artemisa Province") provinces.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:2-24) Patients in [Bahía Honda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bah%C3%ADa_Honda,_Cuba "Bahía Honda, Cuba") were evacuated to a local clinic after fearing flooding.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:3-25)

On August 28, hurricane warnings and [storm surge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_surge "Storm surge") warnings were issued for portions of the Florida's west coast.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-EOTS_warnings-11) On August 29, the [Storm Prediction Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_Prediction_Center "Storm Prediction Center") issued a Day 1 convective outlook highlighting a level 2/slight risk of severe weather for portions of Florida associated with Idalia, with the SPC also issuing a 5 percent tornado risk.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-26) A Day 2 convective outlook was also issued concerning a level 2/slight risk and a 5 percent tornado risk for portions of Florida, [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)"), [South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina "South Carolina"), and [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina "North Carolina").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-27) A moderate risk of excessive rainfall was also issued by the [Weather Prediction Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Prediction_Center "Weather Prediction Center"), for most of the same areas included in the Day 2 Convective outlook.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-28) A [tornado watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_watch "Tornado watch") was issued for portions of western Florida on August 29, as bands of thunderstorms from Idalia moved inland.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-29)

[Amtrak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amtrak "Amtrak") terminated its two southbound _[Silver Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver\_Service "Silver Service")_ routes in [Jacksonville, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacksonville,_Florida "Jacksonville, Florida") on August 28 and cancelled both routes and its _[Auto Train](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auto\_Train "Auto Train")_ service from August 29 to 30. The _[Palmetto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmetto\_(train) "Palmetto (train)")_ route was truncated to [Washington D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_D.C. "Washington D.C.") as well.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-30) At least 900 flights were cancelled across Florida and Georgia.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:8-31)

The storm brought heavy rainfall to the Yucatán Peninsula.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-62) As Idalia became a tropical storm, [Cayman Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayman_Islands "Cayman Islands") were lashed with rough seas, waves up to 6 feet (1.8 m).[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-63) The islands also received cooler weather.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-64) Flooding occurred in [Güira de Melena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%BCira_de_Melena "Güira de Melena") and [Guanimar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guanimar "Guanimar") in Cuba, and high winds hit [Pinar del Río Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinar_del_R%C3%ADo_Province "Pinar del Río Province").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:2-24)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:3-25) Rainfall reached 4 inches (100 mm) across portions of the country.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-65)

### United States

See also: [List of United States tornadoes from July to August 2023 §August 30 event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_tornadoes_from_July_to_August_2023#August_30_event "List of United States tornadoes from July to August 2023")

As of September 25, assessed damage reached $704.1 million across Florida and Georgia. In Florida, at least 21,252 insurance claims were made with losses totaling $216.1 million.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-66) Agricultural losses reached $447 million in the state.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-67) Damage in Georgia exceeded $41 million.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-68) Estimates of total damage across the Southeastern United States vary widely from various insurance companies and catastrophe modelers. Early calculations showed possibilities of damage exceeding $9 billion and potentially reaching $20 billion,[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-69)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-70) though these tempered as time passed. On September 4, [Moody's Analytics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moody's_Analytics "Moody's Analytics") reported private insured losses at $3–5 billion with a "best estimate" of $3.5 billion. They indicated losses attached to the [National Flood Insurance Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Flood_Insurance_Program "National Flood Insurance Program") would reach $500 million. [Verisk Analytics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verisk_Analytics "Verisk Analytics") placed the same metric at $2.5–4 billion. Karen Clark & Co. estimated losses at $2.2 billion on September 1.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-71) Of this, $2 billion was from wind-related damage and $210 million from storm surge.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-72) Regularly improving building codes across Florida are attributed with lesser damage as structures are more able to withstand the effects of hurricanes. Homes built on stilts and with properly secured roofs suffered minimal damage while older structures were severely affected.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-73)

At least twelve people were killed in incidents related to the hurricane: four in Florida, three in New Jersey and North Carolina, and one each in Delaware and Georgia.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-TCR-1)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:11-74)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:12-75)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:13-76)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:14-77)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:15-78)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:16-79)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:17-80)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:18-81)

#### Florida

As Idalia was nearing landfall on the morning of August 30, an [extreme wind warning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extreme_wind_warning "Extreme wind warning") was issued for portions of the Gulf Coast of Florida, including [Steinhatchee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steinhatchee,_Florida "Steinhatchee, Florida") and [Perry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perry,_Florida "Perry, Florida").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-82)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-83)

Idalia made landfall in [Keaton Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keaton_Beach,_Florida "Keaton Beach, Florida"), with sustained winds of 115 mph (185 km/h), causing severe damage in the area.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-84) Water levels near [Cedar Key](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Key,_Florida "Cedar Key, Florida") reached 6.8 ft (2.1 m), and the storm surge water level was at 8.9 feet (2.7 m).[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:6-36)[Tampa Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tampa_Bay "Tampa Bay") and [Clearwater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clearwater,_Florida "Clearwater, Florida") experienced over 3 ft (0.91 m) of storm surge.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-85)[US 41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_41_in_Florida "U.S. Route 41 in Florida") bridges in [Port Charlotte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Charlotte,_Florida "Port Charlotte, Florida") and [Punta Gorda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punta_Gorda,_Florida "Punta Gorda, Florida") were closed due to flooding.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:6-36) Waves crashed over the northbound side of the [Howard Frankland Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Frankland_Bridge "Howard Frankland Bridge"), partially flooding the bridge.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-86) Across [Pasco County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasco_County,_Florida "Pasco County, Florida"), an estimated 2,000 homes were damaged as up to 5 ft (1.5 m) of water inundated structures. Roughly 150 people required rescue during the storm.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-87) Two men were killed in traffic accidents while driving in hazardous conditions in Pasco and [Alachua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alachua_County,_Florida "Alachua County, Florida") counties respectively.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:11-74)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:12-75) In [Hernando Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hernando_Beach,_Florida "Hernando Beach, Florida"), storm surge prevented firefighters from reaching an unoccupied house which caught fire, forcing neighbors to try to contain the fire with garden hoses to prevent the fire from spreading.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-88)

Idalia caused widespread wind damage in Suwannee county as the eyewall passed over. Many barns and carports were destroyed, along with a few other farm buildings. Wind gusts in [Dowling Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dowling_Park,_Florida "Dowling Park, Florida") were estimated to be as high as 100 miles per hour (160 km/h), and wind gusts were estimated at over 110 miles per hour (180 km/h) in a small area around the [Suwannee River.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suwannee_River "Suwannee River")[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-89)

At least 75 people were rescued from flooded areas near [St. Petersburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Petersburg,_Florida "St. Petersburg, Florida").[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-90)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-91) The [Governor's Mansion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Governor's_Mansion "Florida Governor's Mansion") in [Tallahassee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tallahassee,_Florida "Tallahassee, Florida") was struck by a falling oak tree, but no injuries or serious damage was reported.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-92) A gas transmission line in Tallahassee gave out, forcing residents within a quarter-mile of it to evacuate.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-93) Waves partially destroyed the balusters of [Memorial Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Park_(Jacksonville) "Memorial Park (Jacksonville)") in Jacksonville, which had been repaired following damage caused by [Hurricane Irma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Irma "Hurricane Irma") just under six years earlier.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-94) Off of [Merritt Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merritt_Island,_Florida "Merritt Island, Florida"), a man went missing while windsurfing in the [Banana River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banana_River "Banana River") and his body was found on September 2. Because he drowned while the area was under a tropical storm warning, it has been classified as a hurricane-related death.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:13-76)

At least 278,000 customers lost power and more than 200 flights were cancelled across several airlines in Florida.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-95)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:7-43)

On September 5, a man in [Dixie County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dixie_County,_Florida "Dixie County, Florida") was killed while clearing debris with a tractor when he was struck by a falling tree.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:14-77)

#### Georgia

Georgia") area.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-96) Downed power lines closed a portion of [I-75](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_75_in_Georgia "Interstate 75 in Georgia") south of Valdosta.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:8-31) One man was killed in Valdosta after a tree fell as the man helped two sheriff's deputies clear debris from a road.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:15-78)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:10-97) Rainfall in the Valdosta area reached 5.5 in (140 mm).[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-98) In addition, [I-75](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_75_in_Georgia "Interstate 75 in Georgia") in the Valdosta area was shut down.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-99) Damage in [Lowndes County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowndes_County,_Georgia "Lowndes County, Georgia") was estimated at $20 million, with 1,127 homes damaged.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-100)[American Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Airlines "American Airlines") suspended operations at [Savannah/Hilton Head International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savannah/Hilton_Head_International_Airport "Savannah/Hilton Head International Airport"),[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:9-44) and Hoboken Elementary School in [Hoboken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoboken,_Georgia "Hoboken, Georgia") had portions of its roof ripped off.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-101) A weak EF0 tornado passed west of [Brunswick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunswick,_Georgia "Brunswick, Georgia"), damaging a traffic light and downing numerous trees. An EF1 tornado then struck the town minutes later, throwing a tree branch through the windshield of a pickup truck, blowing the top off of a storage shed, knocking down a small billboard, and snapping or uprooting numerous trees. Another short-lived EF1 tornado to the east of Brunswick in [St. Simons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Simons,_Georgia "St. Simons, Georgia") also snapped and uprooted trees. An additional short-lived EF0 tornado occurred northwest of [Fleming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fleming,_Georgia "Fleming, Georgia") as well.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-DAT-102) Over 190,000 customers in Georgia lost power.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-103) In [Bulloch County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulloch_County,_Georgia "Bulloch County, Georgia"), four county roads were severely damaged by more than 8 in (200 mm) of rain causing flooding throughout the county. Bulloch's Public Works and Transportation Director, Dink Butler, who is responsible for overseeing county roads, estimated the cost of damages to be at $360,080.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-104)

#### South Carolina

A very brief EF0 tornado in [Goose Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goose_Creek,_South_Carolina "Goose Creek, South Carolina") flipped a car on [US 52](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_52_in_South_Carolina "U.S. Route 52 in South Carolina"), injuring two people.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-DAT-102)[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-105) Four other tornadoes struck the state as well. An EF1 tornado struck a wooded area northeast of [Turbeville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turbeville,_South_Carolina "Turbeville, South Carolina"), while an EF0 tornado moved southeast through [Mount Pleasant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Pleasant,_South_Carolina "Mount Pleasant, South Carolina"), causing minor damage and crossed over [Wando High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wando_High_School "Wando High School").[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-106)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-107) The [Francis Marion National Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Marion_National_Forest "Francis Marion National Forest") was struck by an EF1 tornado which left trees uprooted and snapped.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-108)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-DAT-102) In [North Myrtle Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Myrtle_Beach,_South_Carolina "North Myrtle Beach, South Carolina"), a waterspout came ashore as an EF0 tornado and caused damage to a neighborhood.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-109) Storm surge breached [The Battery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Battery_(Charleston) "The Battery (Charleston)"), a historical defensive seawall and promenade in [Charleston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charleston,_South_Carolina "Charleston, South Carolina"), causing flooding in the downtown. Further south down the coast in [Edisto Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edisto_Beach,_South_Carolina "Edisto Beach, South Carolina"), a dune was also breached by storm surge, causing flooding within the town.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-110)

Beginning on September 3, heavy rains from Idalia in the [Midlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midlands_of_South_Carolina "Midlands of South Carolina") began flooding low-lying areas along the [Edisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edisto_River "Edisto River") and [Combahee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combahee_River "Combahee River") rivers in [Colleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colleton_County,_South_Carolina "Colleton County, South Carolina") and [Dorchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorchester_County,_South_Carolina "Dorchester County, South Carolina") counties, with water levels peaking at 14.5 feet (4.4 m) at a river gauge at [Givhans Ferry State Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Givhans_Ferry_State_Park "Givhans Ferry State Park").[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-111) The flooding caused one person to be rescued from a home in Givhans.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-112)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-113)

#### North Carolina

Three tornadoes struck the state. An EF0 tornado damaged a veterinary hospital and two other buildings in [St. James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._James,_North_Carolina "St. James, North Carolina"). An EF1 tornado struck a wooded area in [Old Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Town,_Brunswick_County,_North_Carolina "Old Town, Brunswick County, North Carolina"), while in [Myrtle Grove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myrtle_Grove,_North_Carolina "Myrtle Grove, North Carolina"), a waterspout moved ashore and became an EF1 tornado, damaging two buildings and causing a tree to fall on an SUV, injuring the driver.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-114) One person drowned due to rip currents along the coast of [Avon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avon,_North_Carolina "Avon, North Carolina") on September 4.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:18-81)

#### Elsewhere

Rip currents produced by the remnants of Idalia across the Eastern United States resulted in numerous rescues. Beaches were packed with people enjoying the [Labor Day Weekend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labor_Day_Weekend "Labor Day Weekend"). One person drowned off [Rehoboth Beach, Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rehoboth_Beach,_Delaware "Rehoboth Beach, Delaware"), on September 3.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:17-80) At least a dozen people required rescue along the New Jersey coast. Three people died in the state on September 4: one in [Beach Haven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beach_Haven,_New_Jersey "Beach Haven, New Jersey"), one in [Belmar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmar,_New_Jersey "Belmar, New Jersey"), and the third in [Seaside Heights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seaside_Heights,_New_Jersey "Seaside Heights, New Jersey").[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:16-79)[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-115)

Idalia was also associated with an unusual movement of [American Flamingos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Flamingo "American Flamingo"), with a large number of flamingos seen in [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), and flamingos seen as far north as [Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio "Ohio") and [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania").[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-116)

### Bermuda

On September 2, the Department of Marine and Ports Services announced that ferries were suspended until weather conditions improved, [BELCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bermuda_Electric_Light_Company "Bermuda Electric Light Company") announced that Idalia had caused over 6,000 power outages, and the Department of Public Transportation announced the temporary suspension of bus services.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-117) Idalia also caused all flights between [L.F. Wade International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L.F._Wade_International_Airport "L.F. Wade International Airport") and North America to be cancelled or delayed on September 2, with some flights also being affected the following day.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-118)

Hurricane Idalia's wind history.

### United States

On August 31, 2023, President Joe Biden said that he had spoken to Florida Governor Ron DeSantis and other governors about Idalia and that he had approved of their requests for disaster and emergency declarations.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-119)

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/P20230902OC-1140_%2853234993953%29.jpg/250px-P20230902OC-1140_%2853234993953%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:P20230902OC-1140_(53234993953).jpg)

President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") addressing the impacts of the storm in [Live Oak, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_Oak,_Florida "Live Oak, Florida")

#### Florida

On August 30, Governor Ron DeSantis visited Perry and gave a press conference update on the state's response to the storm, where he spoke alongside several state and local officials.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-120) President Biden announced that he had directed FEMA Administrator [Deanne Criswell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deanne_Criswell "Deanne Criswell") to fly to Florida and meet with DeSantis and that up to 1,500 federal personnel as well as 900 members of the [Coast Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Coast_Guard "United States Coast Guard") were being sent to respond to the hurricane's impacts.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-121)[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-122)

On September 2, President Biden, First Lady [Jill Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jill_Biden "Jill Biden"), and FEMA Administrator Deanne Criswell, landed at [Gainesville Regional Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gainesville_Regional_Airport "Gainesville Regional Airport") before embarking on an aerial tour of affected areas within the state. Biden then visited Suwannee Pineview Elementary School in [Live Oak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_Oak,_Florida "Live Oak, Florida") where he was briefed on the damage caused by the storm. Biden met with residents of Live Oak as well as Live Oak Mayor Frank Davis and Senator [Rick Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Scott "Rick Scott") among other officials.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-123)

FEMA opened up six temporary Disaster and Recovery Centers across Dixie, [Levy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levy_County,_Florida "Levy County, Florida"), [Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton_County,_Florida "Hamilton County, Florida"), [Suwannee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suwannee_County,_Florida "Suwannee County, Florida"), [Madison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_County,_Florida "Madison County, Florida"), and [Lafayette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lafayette_County,_Florida "Lafayette County, Florida") counties.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-124) Fourteen counties; [Citrus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citrus_County,_Florida "Citrus County, Florida"), [Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_County,_Florida "Columbia County, Florida"), Dixie, [Gilchrist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilchrist_County,_Florida "Gilchrist County, Florida"), Hamilton, [Hernando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hernando_County,_Florida "Hernando County, Florida"), [Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_County,_Florida "Jefferson County, Florida"), Lafayette, Levy, Madison, Pasco, Pinellas, Suwannee, and [Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_County,_Florida "Taylor County, Florida"), were made eligible for Individual, Critical Needs, Clean and Sanitize, and Disaster Unemployment Assistance.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-125)

The [Small Business Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small_Business_Administration "Small Business Administration") made available Business Physical Disaster, Economic Injury Disaster, and Home Disaster loans available to Citrus, Columbia, Dixie, Gilchrist, Hamilton, Hernando, Jefferson, Lafayette, Levy, Madison, Pasco, Pinellas, Suwannee, and Taylor counties. Meanwhile, Alachua, [Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baker_County,_Florida "Baker County, Florida"), [Hillsborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillsborough_County,_Florida "Hillsborough County, Florida"), [Leon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leon_County,_Florida "Leon County, Florida"), [Marion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marion_County,_Florida "Marion County, Florida"), [Polk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polk_County,_Florida "Polk County, Florida"), [Sumter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sumter_County,_Florida "Sumter County, Florida"), [Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_County,_Florida "Union County, Florida"), and [Wakulla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wakulla_County,_Florida "Wakulla County, Florida") counties were only eligible for Economic Injury Disaster loans.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-126)

The hurricane began an apparent American Flamingo population boom within the state, as wildlife experts believe many of the birds that were brought from the Caribbean and Yucatán Peninsula into the United States by Idalia's winds did not leave the state like they did in other parts of the country and instead settled down. While flamingos are native to South Florida, they have not existed in significant numbers since the 19th century, when hunting drove them out of the state, but according to [Audubon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audubon "Audubon") who conducted a census on the flamingo population in February, finding 101 birds, they have a chance to reassert themselves in Florida.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-127)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-128)[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-129)

#### Georgia

On September 1, Governor Brian Kemp toured Valdosta with Georgia First Lady [Marty Kemp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Kemp "Marty Kemp") and other state officials to survey damage from Idalia. While in Valdosta, [Georgia Emergency Management and Homeland Security Agency Director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Emergency_Management_and_Homeland_Security_Agency "Georgia Emergency Management and Homeland Security Agency") Chris Stallings announced that the state had requested federal assistance from FEMA for the clean-up efforts within the state.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-:10-97)

The SBA declared [Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cook_County,_Georgia "Cook County, Georgia"), [Glynn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glynn_County,_Georgia "Glynn County, Georgia"), and [Lowndes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowndes_County,_Georgia "Lowndes County, Georgia") counties eligible for Physical and Economic Injury Disaster Loans due being approved federal disaster relief funds from FEMA due to President Biden approving a major disaster declaration for the counties, which also made those counties eligible for Individual and Public Assistance from FEMA.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-130)[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-131) Meanwhile, [Berrien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berrien_County,_Georgia "Berrien County, Georgia"), [Brooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooks_County,_Georgia "Brooks County, Georgia"), [Camden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camden_County,_Georgia "Camden County, Georgia"), [Colquitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colquitt_County,_Georgia "Colquitt County, Georgia"), [Echols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Echols_County,_Georgia "Echols County, Georgia"), [Lanier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lanier_County,_Georgia "Lanier County, Georgia"), [McIntosh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McIntosh_County,_Georgia "McIntosh County, Georgia"), [Tift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tift_County,_Georgia "Tift County, Georgia"), and [Wayne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_County,_Georgia "Wayne County, Georgia") counties were made eligible to apply only for Economic Injury Disaster Loans.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-132) The [United States Department of Agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Agriculture "United States Department of Agriculture") has also approved of financial aid to farmers in Berrien County with crop damage.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Idalia#cite_note-133)

The National Hurricane Center and Central Pacific Hurricane Center's Tropical Cyclone Reports (TCRs) contain information on all tropical (and subtropical) cyclones that have occurred within the Atlantic, eastern Pacific, and central Pacific basins, including synoptic history, meteorological statistics, casualties and damages, and the post-analysis best track (six-hourly positions and intensities). As of 2023, comprehensive versions of these reports are provided for all tropical cyclones in which coastal watches and warnings were in effect or direct fatalities were reported, and for other select storms with significant public or research interest (e.g., storms investigated via research field campaigns). Otherwise, abbreviated TCRs are produced that include a short description of the cyclone’s origin, justification of the analyzed maximum winds and minimum pressure, noteworthy statistics, and the post-analysis best track. The abbreviated TCRs also contain the full suite of tables and figures that are included in the comprehensive reports. Tropical cyclones include depressions, storms, and hurricanes. Tropical depressions included below are those that did not reach tropical storm strength. Potential tropical cyclones listed below are disturbances that NHC issued advisories on based on their threat to land, but which failed to develop into tropical cyclones.

The National Hurricane Center and Central Pacific Hurricane Center's Tropical Cyclone Reports (TCRs) contain information on all tropical (and subtropical) cyclones that have occurred within the Atlantic, eastern Pacific, and central Pacific basins, including synoptic history, meteorological statistics, casualties and damages, and the post-analysis best track (six-hourly positions and intensities). As of 2023, comprehensive versions of these reports are provided for all tropical cyclones in which coastal watches and warnings were in effect or direct fatalities were reported, and for other select storms with significant public or research interest (e.g., storms investigated via research field campaigns). Otherwise, abbreviated TCRs are produced that include a short description of the cyclone’s origin, justification of the analyzed maximum winds and minimum pressure, noteworthy statistics, and the post-analysis best track. The abbreviated TCRs also contain the full suite of tables and figures that are included in the comprehensive reports. Tropical cyclones include depressions, storms, and hurricanes. Tropical depressions included below are those that did not reach tropical storm strength. Potential tropical cyclones listed below are disturbances that NHC issued advisories on based on their threat to land, but which failed to develop into tropical cyclones.

[Fast Facts](https://coast.noaa.gov/coastal-facts)/ Hurricane Costs

# Hurricane Costs

Of all recorded weather disasters in U.S. history, tropical cyclones—known as hurricanes when occurring in the North Atlantic, central North Pacific, and Eastern North Pacific Oceans—have caused the most deaths and destruction. While much of the information on this page focuses on hurricanes, some of the numbers account for total weather disasters, including flooding, severe storms, and wildfires.

##### 115

The number of weather and climate disasters in the U.S. from 2020 to 2024 with losses exceeding $1 billion.

##### $2.915 trillion

The total approximate cost of damages from weather and climate disasters in the U.S. from 1980 to present (as of February 2025).

##### 23

The average annual number of weather and climate disasters from 2020 to 2024. In 2024 alone, the U.S. experienced 27 billion-dollar disasters.

##### 2024: Above Average

The 27 billion-dollar disasters in 2024 resulted in $182.7 billion in damages–higher than the average annual amount of events (23) and the average annual cost ($149.3 billion) for the past five years.   
  
 2024 was also the warmest year in NOAA’s global temperature record, which dates back to 1850. Antarctic sea ice extent was second lowest on record in both February (when the annual minimum occurs) and September (when the annual maximum occurs).

##### Hurricanes Helene and Milton: Historic Damage and Destruction

Making landfall near Perry, Florida, on September 26, 2024, **Hurricane Helene**—with sustained winds of 140 miles per hour—was the strongest hurricane on record to strike the Big Bend region of Florida and the third hurricane to hit that region in just over a year. It also caused billions of dollars in damage to Georgia's agriculture sector. Helene's most severe impacts were from the historic rainfall (up to over 30 inches) and record-breaking flooding across much of western North Carolina. Asheville and many surrounding cities and communities were heavily impacted, as were southwestern Virginia and eastern Tennessee.   
  
 Helene was the deadliest Atlantic hurricane since Maria (2017), and the deadliest to strike the U.S. mainland since Katrina (2005). Helene’s total costs were $78.7 billion.   
  
 With 120 mile-per-hour sustained winds, **Hurricane Milton** made landfall near Siesta Key, Florida, on October 9, 2024. A storm surge of up to 10 feet caused damage from along the Gulf coast, and the hurricane spawned dozens of highly destructive tornadoes across southern Florida. Total costs for Milton were $34.3 billion.

##### 2023: Breaking Many Records

The year 2023 broke multiple weather and climate records. Earth had its warmest July on record. July also set a record for the highest monthly sea surface temperature anomaly (+1.78°F or +0.99°C) of any month in NOAA’s 174-year record. According to the NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information’s Global Annual Temperature Outlook, it is almost certain (over 99 percent) that the year 2023 will rank among the five warmest years on record, with a nearly 50-percent probability that 2023 will rank warmest on record.   
  
 In August, Tropical Storm Hilary made history as the first tropical storm to hit Southern California in 84 years. Rainfalls for Hilary broke virtually all daily rainfall records for the area.   
  
 In total, 28 weather and climate disasters with losses exceeding $1 billion each affected the U.S. in 2023. The combined total cost of these 2023 disasters is $93.1 billion. Only one other year (2017) had more billion-dollar disasters in the first six months, and 2023 was second only to 2021 for total damage costs through the first half of any year since 1980.

##### 2022: Year in Review

In 2022, there were 18 separate billion-dollar weather and climate disasters. The total cost for these events was over $165 billion, making this the third most costly year on record at the time.

##### 2020: New Annual Record

2020 set a new record for events, with 22 billion-dollar weather and climate disasters—shattering the previous annual record of 16 events in 2011 and 2017.

##### Tropical Cyclones: The Highest Costs

Of the 403 billion-dollar weather disasters since 1980 (as of December 31, 2024), tropical cyclones (or hurricanes) have caused the most damage: over $1.5 trillion total, with an average cost of $23 billion per event. They are also responsible for the highest number of deaths: 7,211 since 1980.

##### Harvey, Irma, and Maria: Making History

The 2017 Atlantic hurricane season was among the most intense ever recorded. The combined costs for Harvey, Irma, and Maria totaled $339.2 billion.  
  
**Hurricane Harvey:** Harvey was the most significant tropical cyclone rainfall event ever recorded in U.S. history, both in scope and peak rainfall amounts. The highest storm total rainfall report from Harvey was 60.58 inches. Prior to Hurricanes Irma and Maria, Harvey became the deadliest U.S. hurricane in terms of direct deaths since Sandy (2012) and the deadliest hurricane to hit Texas since 1919. It was the first category 4 hurricane to make landfall in Texas since 1961, and the first category 4 to make landfall in the U.S. since 2004. Harvey lasted 117 hours, beating the previous record for duration of Hurricane Fern in 1971.  
  
**Hurricane Irma:** With maximum winds of 185 miles per hour, Irma became the strongest storm on record to exist in the Atlantic Ocean outside of the Caribbean and Gulf of America. It sustained those maximum winds speeds for 37 hours and spent three consecutive days as a category 5 hurricane—making it the longest of any cyclone in the world since 1932 to maintain that intensity. The occurrences of Harvey and Irma—making landfall within two weeks of each other—were the first time in recorded history that two category 4 or higher hurricanes struck the U.S. mainland in the same year.  
  
**Hurricane Maria:** Maria was the first category 5 hurricane ever to make landfall in Dominica, and the strongest hurricane to make landfall in Puerto Rico since 1928. It was the deadliest of 2017’s three major storm, with over 2,900 fatalities.

# Hurricane Costs

Of all recorded weather disasters in U.S. history, tropical cyclones—known as hurricanes when occurring in the North Atlantic, central North Pacific, and Eastern North Pacific Oceans—have caused the most deaths and destruction. While much of the information on this page focuses on hurricanes, some of the numbers account for total weather disasters, including flooding, severe storms, and wildfires.

##### 115

The number of weather and climate disasters in the U.S. from 2020 to 2024 with losses exceeding $1 billion.

##### $2.915 trillion

The total approximate cost of damages from weather and climate disasters in the U.S. from 1980 to present (as of February 2025).

##### 23

The average annual number of weather and climate disasters from 2020 to 2024. In 2024 alone, the U.S. experienced 27 billion-dollar disasters.

##### 2024: Above Average

The 27 billion-dollar disasters in 2024 resulted in $182.7 billion in damages–higher than the average annual amount of events (23) and the average annual cost ($149.3 billion) for the past five years.   
  
 2024 was also the warmest year in NOAA’s global temperature record, which dates back to 1850. Antarctic sea ice extent was second lowest on record in both February (when the annual minimum occurs) and September (when the annual maximum occurs).

##### Hurricanes Helene and Milton: Historic Damage and Destruction

Making landfall near Perry, Florida, on September 26, 2024, **Hurricane Helene**—with sustained winds of 140 miles per hour—was the strongest hurricane on record to strike the Big Bend region of Florida and the third hurricane to hit that region in just over a year. It also caused billions of dollars in damage to Georgia's agriculture sector. Helene's most severe impacts were from the historic rainfall (up to over 30 inches) and record-breaking flooding across much of western North Carolina. Asheville and many surrounding cities and communities were heavily impacted, as were southwestern Virginia and eastern Tennessee.   
  
 Helene was the deadliest Atlantic hurricane since Maria (2017), and the deadliest to strike the U.S. mainland since Katrina (2005). Helene’s total costs were $78.7 billion.   
  
 With 120 mile-per-hour sustained winds, **Hurricane Milton** made landfall near Siesta Key, Florida, on October 9, 2024. A storm surge of up to 10 feet caused damage from along the Gulf coast, and the hurricane spawned dozens of highly destructive tornadoes across southern Florida. Total costs for Milton were $34.3 billion.

##### 2023: Breaking Many Records

The year 2023 broke multiple weather and climate records. Earth had its warmest July on record. July also set a record for the highest monthly sea surface temperature anomaly (+1.78°F or +0.99°C) of any month in NOAA’s 174-year record. According to the NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information’s Global Annual Temperature Outlook, it is almost certain (over 99 percent) that the year 2023 will rank among the five warmest years on record, with a nearly 50-percent probability that 2023 will rank warmest on record.   
  
 In August, Tropical Storm Hilary made history as the first tropical storm to hit Southern California in 84 years. Rainfalls for Hilary broke virtually all daily rainfall records for the area.   
  
 In total, 28 weather and climate disasters with losses exceeding $1 billion each affected the U.S. in 2023. The combined total cost of these 2023 disasters is $93.1 billion. Only one other year (2017) had more billion-dollar disasters in the first six months, and 2023 was second only to 2021 for total damage costs through the first half of any year since 1980.

##### 2022: Year in Review

In 2022, there were 18 separate billion-dollar weather and climate disasters. The total cost for these events was over $165 billion, making this the third most costly year on record at the time.

##### 2020: New Annual Record

2020 set a new record for events, with 22 billion-dollar weather and climate disasters—shattering the previous annual record of 16 events in 2011 and 2017.

##### Tropical Cyclones: The Highest Costs

Of the 403 billion-dollar weather disasters since 1980 (as of December 31, 2024), tropical cyclones (or hurricanes) have caused the most damage: over $1.5 trillion total, with an average cost of $23 billion per event. They are also responsible for the highest number of deaths: 7,211 since 1980.

##### Harvey, Irma, and Maria: Making History

The 2017 Atlantic hurricane season was among the most intense ever recorded. The combined costs for Harvey, Irma, and Maria totaled $339.2 billion.  
  
**Hurricane Harvey:** Harvey was the most significant tropical cyclone rainfall event ever recorded in U.S. history, both in scope and peak rainfall amounts. The highest storm total rainfall report from Harvey was 60.58 inches. Prior to Hurricanes Irma and Maria, Harvey became the deadliest U.S. hurricane in terms of direct deaths since Sandy (2012) and the deadliest hurricane to hit Texas since 1919. It was the first category 4 hurricane to make landfall in Texas since 1961, and the first category 4 to make landfall in the U.S. since 2004. Harvey lasted 117 hours, beating the previous record for duration of Hurricane Fern in 1971.  
  
**Hurricane Irma:** With maximum winds of 185 miles per hour, Irma became the strongest storm on record to exist in the Atlantic Ocean outside of the Caribbean and Gulf of America. It sustained those maximum winds speeds for 37 hours and spent three consecutive days as a category 5 hurricane—making it the longest of any cyclone in the world since 1932 to maintain that intensity. The occurrences of Harvey and Irma—making landfall within two weeks of each other—were the first time in recorded history that two category 4 or higher hurricanes struck the U.S. mainland in the same year.  
  
**Hurricane Maria:** Maria was the first category 5 hurricane ever to make landfall in Dominica, and the strongest hurricane to make landfall in Puerto Rico since 1928. It was the deadliest of 2017’s three major storm, with over 2,900 fatalities.

The 2022 Atlantic hurricane season officially ends on November 30, but the impact of Hurricanes Ian, Nicole and Fiona — which brought extensive damage to Florida’s coast and Puerto Rico, respectively — will continue to be felt long after the season is over.

In total, this hurricane season produced 14 named storms (winds of 39 mph or greater), of which eight became hurricanes (winds of 74 mph or greater) and two intensified to major hurricanes with winds reaching 111 mph or greater. An average hurricane season has 14 named storms, seven hurricanes and three major hurricanes.

![Image 7: The list of 14 named storms that have occurred during the 2022 Atlantic Hurricane Season. The season officially ends November 30.](https://www.noaa.gov/sites/default/files/2022-11/GRAPHIC-2022-Hurricane-Season-Conclusion-Names-113022.png)

The list of 14 named storms that have occurred during the 2022 Atlantic Hurricane Season. The season officially ends November 30.(NOAA)

[Download Image](https://www.noaa.gov/media/image_download/2ff4333f-e68b-415a-8c3f-5d874ee77458)

The 2022 season saw three hurricane landfalls along the coast of the U.S. mainland. Hurricane Ian made landfall first as a Category 4 storm in Cayo Costa, Florida, and again as a Category 1 in Georgetown, South Carolina. As a Category 4 with 150 mph maximum sustained winds, Hurricane Ian tied for the fifth-strongest hurricane ever to make landfall in the U.S. Hurricane Nicole made landfall as a Category 1 in north Hutchinson Island, Florida.

Hurricane Fiona made landfall outside of the mainland U.S. as a Category 1 near Punta Tocon, Puerto Rico.

“I commend NOAA’s dedicated scientists, hurricane hunter pilots and forecasters who worked diligently to help American communities become hurricane resilient and Climate-Ready for the impacts of this hurricane season and the years to come,” said Secretary of Commerce Gina Raimondo.

This unique season was defined by a rare mid-season pause in storms that scientists preliminarily believe was caused by increased wind shear and suppressed atmospheric moisture high over the Atlantic Ocean. After a quiet period in August, activity ramped up in September with seven named storms, including the two major hurricanes — Fiona and Ian — seen this season. The season also included a rare late-season storm with Hurricane Nicole making landfall on November 10 along the east coast of Florida.

“Forecasters at NOAA’s [National Weather Service](https://www.weather.gov/) and its [National Hurricane Center](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/) issued earlier forecasts with increasing accuracy this season,” said NOAA Administrator Rick Spinrad, Ph.D. “These improved forecasts coupled with critical NOAA data and services undoubtedly led to the better protection of life and property.”

National Hurricane Center forecasts were aided by the [experimental peak storm surge graphic](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/productexamples/Peak_Storm_Surge_Forecast.shtml), which allowed forecasters to more accurately communicate the severity of expected storm surge levels produced by landfalling storms, such as Hurricane Ian. Additionally, NOAA’s [intensity forecasts](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/modelsummary.shtml) showed Hurricane Ian as a major hurricane impacting the coast of Florida from the initial advisory on September 23 through landfall five days later. This advanced lead time gave those in threatened areas more time to prepare and respond.

“The 2022 seasonal activity fell within NOAA’s predicted ranges for named storms and hurricanes in both our pre-season outlook and [updated outlook](https://www.noaa.gov/news-release/noaa-still-expects-above-normal-atlantic-hurricane-season),” said Matthew Rosencrans, lead hurricane forecaster at NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center. “La Niña conditions remained robust throughout the season while the West African Monsoon was only slightly above normal, which both largely aligned with conditions anticipated by the team at NOAA.”

Video summary of all the named storms that formed during the 2022 Atlantic hurricane season. (NOAA)

**NOAA’s hurricane research and response**

This season, [NOAA Hurricane Hunter](https://www.omao.noaa.gov/learn/aircraft-operations/about/hurricane-hunters) aircraft flew over 582 mission hours to collect atmospheric data that is critical to hurricane forecasting and research, passing through the eye of a hurricane 65 times and deploying over 1,700 scientific instruments. NOAA’s Gulfstream IV-SP also flew a research mission from Cabo Verde, Africa, in August. This historic mission was the furthest east NOAA’s Hurricane Hunter airplanes have flown to investigate a developing storm.

Another major first included the successful launch of the [Altius 600 small uncrewed aircraft system](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/news/altius-drone-flies-hurricane-ian/) by scientists from NOAA’s [Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Lab](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/). Scientists launched the instrument from NOAA’s P-3 Hurricane Hunter into the core of Hurricane Ian hours before landfall, transmitting back data of wind speeds as high as 216 mph at an altitude of 2,150 feet.

NOAA's [National Ocean Service](https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/) captured thousands of aerial [overflight images](https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/news/sep22/ngs-storm-imagery-ian.html) after Hurricane Ian. The images helped identify and record more than 6,200 potential pollution risks and assisted the U.S. Coast Guard in clearing pollution from the environment and facilitating marine debris cleanup efforts. A NOAA King Air and Twin Otter aircraft flew over 41 mission hours to support aerial imagery collection for emergency response after Hurricanes Ian and Nicole.  
  
 Forecasters and researchers relied on this invaluable data coupled with [NOAA’s advanced geostationary and polar-orbiting weather satellites](https://www.nesdis.noaa.gov/), [NOAA's weather buoys](https://www.ndbc.noaa.gov/) and other sources before, during and after storms throughout this destructive hurricane season.

While the 2022 season is drawing to a close, now is not the time to let your guard down. The 2023 hurricane season will officially begin on June 1. Take the time to ensure your family is [Weather-Ready](https://www.weather.gov/safety/hurricane) for the season ahead. NOAA’s [Climate Prediction Center](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/), a division of the National Weather Service, will issue its initial 2023 seasonal outlook in May.

The 2022 Atlantic hurricane season officially ends on November 30, but the impact of Hurricanes Ian, Nicole and Fiona — which brought extensive damage to Florida’s coast and Puerto Rico, respectively — will continue to be felt long after the season is over.

In total, this hurricane season produced 14 named storms (winds of 39 mph or greater), of which eight became hurricanes (winds of 74 mph or greater) and two intensified to major hurricanes with winds reaching 111 mph or greater. An average hurricane season has 14 named storms, seven hurricanes and three major hurricanes.

![Image 7: The list of 14 named storms that have occurred during the 2022 Atlantic Hurricane Season. The season officially ends November 30.](https://www.noaa.gov/sites/default/files/2022-11/GRAPHIC-2022-Hurricane-Season-Conclusion-Names-113022.png)

The list of 14 named storms that have occurred during the 2022 Atlantic Hurricane Season. The season officially ends November 30.(NOAA)

[Download Image](https://www.noaa.gov/media/image_download/2ff4333f-e68b-415a-8c3f-5d874ee77458)

The 2022 season saw three hurricane landfalls along the coast of the U.S. mainland. Hurricane Ian made landfall first as a Category 4 storm in Cayo Costa, Florida, and again as a Category 1 in Georgetown, South Carolina. As a Category 4 with 150 mph maximum sustained winds, Hurricane Ian tied for the fifth-strongest hurricane ever to make landfall in the U.S. Hurricane Nicole made landfall as a Category 1 in north Hutchinson Island, Florida.

Hurricane Fiona made landfall outside of the mainland U.S. as a Category 1 near Punta Tocon, Puerto Rico.

“I commend NOAA’s dedicated scientists, hurricane hunter pilots and forecasters who worked diligently to help American communities become hurricane resilient and Climate-Ready for the impacts of this hurricane season and the years to come,” said Secretary of Commerce Gina Raimondo.

This unique season was defined by a rare mid-season pause in storms that scientists preliminarily believe was caused by increased wind shear and suppressed atmospheric moisture high over the Atlantic Ocean. After a quiet period in August, activity ramped up in September with seven named storms, including the two major hurricanes — Fiona and Ian — seen this season. The season also included a rare late-season storm with Hurricane Nicole making landfall on November 10 along the east coast of Florida.

“Forecasters at NOAA’s [National Weather Service](https://www.weather.gov/) and its [National Hurricane Center](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/) issued earlier forecasts with increasing accuracy this season,” said NOAA Administrator Rick Spinrad, Ph.D. “These improved forecasts coupled with critical NOAA data and services undoubtedly led to the better protection of life and property.”

National Hurricane Center forecasts were aided by the [experimental peak storm surge graphic](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/productexamples/Peak_Storm_Surge_Forecast.shtml), which allowed forecasters to more accurately communicate the severity of expected storm surge levels produced by landfalling storms, such as Hurricane Ian. Additionally, NOAA’s [intensity forecasts](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/modelsummary.shtml) showed Hurricane Ian as a major hurricane impacting the coast of Florida from the initial advisory on September 23 through landfall five days later. This advanced lead time gave those in threatened areas more time to prepare and respond.

“The 2022 seasonal activity fell within NOAA’s predicted ranges for named storms and hurricanes in both our pre-season outlook and [updated outlook](https://www.noaa.gov/news-release/noaa-still-expects-above-normal-atlantic-hurricane-season),” said Matthew Rosencrans, lead hurricane forecaster at NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center. “La Niña conditions remained robust throughout the season while the West African Monsoon was only slightly above normal, which both largely aligned with conditions anticipated by the team at NOAA.”

Video summary of all the named storms that formed during the 2022 Atlantic hurricane season. (NOAA)

**NOAA’s hurricane research and response**

This season, [NOAA Hurricane Hunter](https://www.omao.noaa.gov/learn/aircraft-operations/about/hurricane-hunters) aircraft flew over 582 mission hours to collect atmospheric data that is critical to hurricane forecasting and research, passing through the eye of a hurricane 65 times and deploying over 1,700 scientific instruments. NOAA’s Gulfstream IV-SP also flew a research mission from Cabo Verde, Africa, in August. This historic mission was the furthest east NOAA’s Hurricane Hunter airplanes have flown to investigate a developing storm.

Another major first included the successful launch of the [Altius 600 small uncrewed aircraft system](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/news/altius-drone-flies-hurricane-ian/) by scientists from NOAA’s [Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Lab](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/). Scientists launched the instrument from NOAA’s P-3 Hurricane Hunter into the core of Hurricane Ian hours before landfall, transmitting back data of wind speeds as high as 216 mph at an altitude of 2,150 feet.

NOAA's [National Ocean Service](https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/) captured thousands of aerial [overflight images](https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/news/sep22/ngs-storm-imagery-ian.html) after Hurricane Ian. The images helped identify and record more than 6,200 potential pollution risks and assisted the U.S. Coast Guard in clearing pollution from the environment and facilitating marine debris cleanup efforts. A NOAA King Air and Twin Otter aircraft flew over 41 mission hours to support aerial imagery collection for emergency response after Hurricanes Ian and Nicole.  
  
 Forecasters and researchers relied on this invaluable data coupled with [NOAA’s advanced geostationary and polar-orbiting weather satellites](https://www.nesdis.noaa.gov/), [NOAA's weather buoys](https://www.ndbc.noaa.gov/) and other sources before, during and after storms throughout this destructive hurricane season.

While the 2022 season is drawing to a close, now is not the time to let your guard down. The 2023 hurricane season will officially begin on June 1. Take the time to ensure your family is [Weather-Ready](https://www.weather.gov/safety/hurricane) for the season ahead. NOAA’s [Climate Prediction Center](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/), a division of the National Weather Service, will issue its initial 2023 seasonal outlook in May.
