# Hurricanes

[![Image 3: hurricanes peakofseason](https://climatecenter.fsu.edu/images/topics/Atlantic_Hurr_PeakofSeason_2020.png)](https://climatecenter.fsu.edu/images/topics/Atlantic_Hurr_PeakofSeason_2020.png)

The threat of hurricanes is very real for Florida during the six-month long Atlantic hurricane season, which runs from June 1 until November 30. The peak of hurricane season occurs between mid-August and late October, when the waters in the equatorial Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico have warmed enough to help support the development of tropical waves.

A common misconception in Florida is that there are parts of the state that do not get hurricanes. Since 1850, all of Florida’s coastline has been impacted by at least one hurricane. With its long coastline and location, Florida frequently finds itself in the path of these intense storms. The southeast coastline is extremely susceptible to a land-falling hurricane, followed by the panhandle. Areas around Tampa, Jacksonville and the Big Bend do not have as high of a risk of a direct strike from a hurricane but are still susceptible to a landfall each year. Even if the hurricane makes landfall elsewhere in the state, the impacts can be felt hundreds of miles away.

_Tropical Depression_ - A tropical cyclone in which the maximum 1-minute sustained surface wind is 33 knots (38 mph) or less.

_Tropical Storm_ - A tropical cyclone in which the maximum 1-minute sustained surface wind ranges from 34 to 63 knots (39 to 73 mph).

_Hurricane_ - A tropical cyclone in the Atlantic, Caribbean Sea, Gulf of Mexico, or eastern Pacific in which the maximum 1-minute sustained surface wind is 64 knots (74 mph) or greater.

_Major Hurricane_ - A hurricane which reaches Category 3 (sustained winds greater than 110 mph) on the Saffir/Simpson Hurricane Scale.

# **Saffir-Simpson Scale**

The Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Scale, originally developed by Herb Saffir (wind engineer) and Bob Simpson (meteorologist), was used to categorize a hurricane based on its intensity at an indicated time. The scale classified the storm on a scale of one to five based on wind velocity, central pressure and height of storm surge.

Recent hurricanes brought to light some of the issues with trying to categorize hurricanes by so many different factors. Central pressure was not routinely measured from hurricanes prior to 1990. Hurricane size (the diameter of the entire storms), along with the extent of tropical storm force and hurricane force winds, local bathymetry, and forward motion were also not taken into account with the original Saffir-Simpson scale. To help reduce the confusion of the scale, the National Hurricane Center adapted a newer version of Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Scale in 2010, known as the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane **Wind**Scale, in which only the peak winds are now used to categorize a hurricane.

  

**SAFFIR-SIMPSON HURRICANE WIND SCALE**
Category Winds (mph)Damage Summary
1 74 – 95 Very dangerous winds will produce some damage.
2 96 – 110 Extremely dangerous winds will cause extensive damage.
3 111 – 129 Devastating damage will occur.
4 130 – 156 Catastrophic damage will occur.
5> 156 Catastrophic damage will occur.
  

*Adapted from data from the National Hurricane Center’s Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale: [http://www.nhc.noaa.gov/pdf/sshws_table.pdf](http://www.nhc.noaa.gov/pdf/sshws_table.pdf)PDF Document External Link.

# **Impacts**

**Winds** are the most well-known impact from tropical storms and hurricanes. The highest winds occur just outside of the eye (or center) in a region known as the eye-wall. Hurricane force winds can easily damage or destroy mobile homes and other non-permanent structures, often moving them well away from their foundations. Roofs, trees and power lines are also frequently damaged by hurricane force winds. Because of Florida’s flat terrain, strong winds do not rapidly weaken after the storm makes landfall. Hurricane Charley in 2004 moved through the state at 25 mph (nearly twice the typical speed of a landfalling hurricane) and brought hurricane-force winds to Orlando, which was nearly 100 miles away from the point of landfall. The strongest hurricanes can have winds in excess of 155 mph.

**Storm surge** is the term used to describe the wall of water that is pushed toward the shoreline as a hurricane moves onshore. Storm surge combines with the local tide and the battering wind-driven waves to push a large volume of water onto the shore, often resulting in significant damage. In the strongest hurricanes, this storm surge can be as high as 25 feet above normal water levels. The combination of the rising water and pounding waves is often deadly. Approximately 90% of all deaths in hurricanes worldwide are caused by drowning in either the storm surges or flooding caused by intense rainfall. Those living in coastal and near-coastal communities should know if or in which evacuation zone they reside, as well as the elevation of their property.

Florida Evacuation Zone Information: [https://www.floridadisaster.org/knowyourzone/](https://www.floridadisaster.org/knowyourzone/)External Link

If local officials declare an evacuation for your area, move to the nearest evacuation destination outside of the declared zone. You may choose to stay with friends/relatives, at a hotel/motel or at an evacuation shelter.

Florida Evacuation Shelter Information: [http://floridadisaster.org/shelters/](http://floridadisaster.org/shelters/)External Link

**Flooding** from tropical cyclones is not correlated with the intensity of the system but instead with the relative speed of the storm. Slow-moving tropical storms and hurricanes often produce large amounts of rain, which can lead to significant flooding at inland locations. Flooding impacts can occur hundreds of miles away from the center of a storm or from the remnants of a former tropical system.

Flooding from torrential rains can produce a lot of damage. Hurricane Easy in September 1950 dumped an estimated 38.70” of rain on Yankeetown, FL, in a 24-hour period. This amount cannot be counted as an official observation since it was estimated, so the official 24-hour state record rainfall amount (23.38”) came from the outer bands of Hurricane Jeanne in 1980.

Tornadoes associated with tropical systems typically form in the right front quadrant of the storm, relative to the direction of forward motion. If you were looking at the storm like it was a clock, this would be the area from about noon to three o’clock in the direction the storm is moving. While not normally as intense as tornadoes produced by non-tropical severe thunderstorms, these tornadoes often move very fast, at speeds over 50 mph. Another common area of tornadoes in a hurricane is in the far outer rain bands, which can be hundreds of miles away from the center of the storm.

# **Preparing for a Hurricane**

There are a variety of lists to help you prepare for the upcoming hurricane season. The Florida Department of Emergency Management has come up with an interactive website to help you tailor these lists to your own household or business needs. Please take the time to go through the tool and make sure you’re prepared.

Create a Hurricane Plan for:

Your Family: [https://www.floridadisaster.org/family-plan/](https://www.floridadisaster.org/family-plan/)External Link

Your Business: [https://www.floridadisaster.org/business/](https://www.floridadisaster.org/business/)External Link

Roofs, trees and power lines are also frequently damaged by hurricane force winds. Because of Florida’s flat terrain, strong winds do not rapidly weaken after the storm makes landfall. Hurricane Charley in 2004 moved through the state at 25 mph (nearly twice the typical speed of a landfalling hurricane) and brought hurricane-force winds to Orlando, which was nearly 100 miles away from the point of landfall. The strongest hurricanes can have winds in excess of 155 mph.

**Storm surge** is the term used to describe the wall of water that is pushed toward the shoreline as a hurricane moves onshore. Storm surge combines with the local tide and the battering wind-driven waves to push a large volume of water onto the shore, often resulting in significant damage. In the strongest hurricanes, this storm surge can be as high as 25 feet above normal water levels. The combination of the rising water and pounding waves is often deadly. Approximately 90% of all deaths in hurricanes worldwide are caused by drowning in either the storm surges or flooding caused by intense rainfall. Those living in coastal and near-coastal communities should know if or in which evacuation zone they reside, as well as the elevation of their property.

Florida Evacuation Zone Information: [https://www.floridadisaster.org/knowyourzone/](https://www.floridadisaster.org/knowyourzone/)External Link

If local officials declare an evacuation for your area, move to the nearest evacuation destination outside of the declared zone. You may choose to stay with friends/relatives, at a hotel/motel or at an evacuation shelter.

Florida Evacuation Shelter Information: [http://floridadisaster.org/shelters/](http://floridadisaster.org/shelters/)External Link

**Flooding** from tropical cyclones is not correlated with the intensity of the system but instead with the relative speed of the storm. Slow-moving tropical storms and hurricanes often produce large amounts of rain, which can lead to significant flooding at inland locations. Flooding impacts can occur hundreds of miles away from the center of a storm or from the remnants of a former tropical system.

Flooding from torrential rains can produce a lot of damage. Hurricane Easy in September 1950 dumped an estimated 38.70” of rain on Yankeetown, FL, in a 24-hour period. This amount cannot be counted as an official observation since it was estimated, so the official 24-hour state record rainfall amount (23.38”) came from the outer bands of Hurricane Jeanne in 1980.

Tornadoes associated with tropical systems typically form in the right front quadrant of the storm, relative to the direction of forward motion. If you were looking at the storm like it was a clock, this would be the area from about noon to three o’clock in the direction the storm is moving. While not normally as intense as tornadoes produced by non-tropical severe thunderstorms, these tornadoes often move very fast, at speeds over 50 mph. Another common area of tornadoes in a hurricane is in the far outer rain bands, which can be hundreds of miles away from the center of the storm.

# **Preparing for a Hurricane**

There are a variety of lists to help you prepare for the upcoming hurricane season. The Florida Department of Emergency Management has come up with an interactive website to help you tailor these lists to your own household or business needs. Please take the time to go through the tool and make sure you’re prepared.

The **2022 Atlantic hurricane season** was a near-average yet destructive [Atlantic hurricane season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_hurricane_season "Atlantic hurricane season"). Despite having an average number of [named storms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclone_naming "Tropical cyclone naming") and a below average amount of major hurricanes,[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-3) it became the fourth-costliest Atlantic hurricane season on record, behind only [2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2024 Atlantic hurricane season"), [2005](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2005 Atlantic hurricane season"), and [2017](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2017 Atlantic hurricane season"), mostly due to [Hurricane Ian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Ian "Hurricane Ian"). The season officially began on June 1, and ended on November 30. These dates, adopted by convention, historically describe the period in each year when most [subtropical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtropical_cyclone "Subtropical cyclone") or [tropical cyclogenesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclogenesis "Tropical cyclogenesis") occurs in the Atlantic Ocean.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-4) This year's first Atlantic named storm, [Tropical Storm Alex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Alex_(2022) "Tropical Storm Alex (2022)"), developed four days after the start of the season, making this the first season since [2014](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2014 Atlantic hurricane season") not to have a pre-season named storm.

Two systems developed on July 1. [Tropical Storm Bonnie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Bonnie_(2022) "Hurricane Bonnie (2022)") formed and made landfall near the [Costa Rica–Nicaragua border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica%E2%80%93Nicaragua_border "Costa Rica–Nicaragua border"). It then crossed over into the [Pacific basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Pacific_hurricane_season "2022 Pacific hurricane season"), becoming the first to survive the crossover from the Atlantic to the Pacific since [Hurricane Otto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Otto "Hurricane Otto") in [2016](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2016 Atlantic hurricane season"). Also, Tropical Storm Colin formed abruptly and made landfall in [South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina "South Carolina"), before quickly weakening and dissipating the next day. Following this activity, tropical cyclogenesis was suppressed across the basin for several weeks by a combination of increased [wind shear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_shear "Wind shear") and the presence of the [Saharan Air Layer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saharan_Air_Layer "Saharan Air Layer"). This stopped all tropical cyclogenesis in August, the first season to do so since [1997](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Atlantic_hurricane_season "1997 Atlantic hurricane season"), and the first during a [La Niña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Ni%C3%B1a "La Niña"). This pause in activity lasted sixty days, ending when hurricanes Danielle and [Earl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Earl_(2022) "Hurricane Earl (2022)") formed on September 1 and 3 respectively. Danielle become the season's first hurricane; the last season to have its first hurricane develop this late was [2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2013 Atlantic hurricane season").

Activity then increased tremendously towards the end of September as four named storms formed in quick succession. Among them, [Hurricane Fiona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Fiona "Hurricane Fiona") became the season's first major hurricane on September 20, which is about three weeks later than when the first one typically forms.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-EOTS_092022-5) As an extratropical cyclone it became the strongest storm in Canadian history, as measured by [atmospheric pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_pressure "Atmospheric pressure"), and caused significant damage in [Atlantic Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Canada "Atlantic Canada"). Hurricane Ian then became the second major hurricane of the season on September 27 and the only Category 5 of the season on September 28 and inflicted an estimated $113.1 billion in damage to western [Cuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuba "Cuba"), [Southwestern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwest_Florida "Southwest Florida") and [Central Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Florida "Central Florida"), and the [Carolinas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolinas "Carolinas"). [Hurricane Julia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Julia_(2022) "Hurricane Julia (2022)") formed in early October and became the second storm of the season to cross over into the Pacific basin intact after traversing Nicaragua, making this season the first to have more than one crossover system since [1996](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Atlantic_hurricane_season "1996 Atlantic hurricane season"). The last storm in the season, [Hurricane Nicole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Nicole_(2022) "Hurricane Nicole (2022)"), made landfall on the coasts of the Bahamas and Florida. It was the first November hurricane to make landfall in Florida since [Kate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Kate_(1985) "Hurricane Kate (1985)") in [1985](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1985_Atlantic_hurricane_season "1985 Atlantic hurricane season"), and caused about $1 billion in damage in areas devastated by Ian six weeks earlier. Tropical cyclones during this season collectively caused at least 304 deaths and more than $117.7 billion in damage, making it one of the costliest seasons on record.

Most forecasting agencies anticipated a well-above average season due to warmer-than-normal [sea surface temperatures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_surface_temperature "Sea surface temperature") and a favorable [El Niño–Southern Oscillation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Ni%C3%B1o%E2%80%93Southern_Oscillation "El Niño–Southern Oscillation") pattern, limiting the chances of [El Niño](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Ni%C3%B1o "El Niño") developing. While conducive conditions such as warmer sea surface temperatures and a La Niña came to fruition, the unfavorable wind shear pattern with drier air and Saharan Air Layer suppressed tropical cyclogenesis through most of July and the entirety of August, with the latter typically being among the most active climatologically.

In advance of, and during, each hurricane season, several [forecasts of hurricane activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclone_seasonal_forecasting "Tropical cyclone seasonal forecasting") are issued by national meteorological services, scientific agencies, and noted hurricane experts. These include forecasters from the United States [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Oceanic_and_Atmospheric_Administration "National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration") (NOAA)'s [Climate Prediction Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_Prediction_Center "Climate Prediction Center"), Tropical Storm Risk (TSR), the United Kingdom's [Met Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Met_Office "Met Office") (UKMO), and Philip J. Klotzbach and their associates at [Colorado State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_University "Colorado State University") (CSU). The forecasts include weekly and monthly changes in significant factors that help determine the number of tropical storms, hurricanes, and major hurricanes within a particular year. According to NOAA and CSU, the average [Atlantic hurricane season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_hurricane_season "Atlantic hurricane season") between 1991 and 2020 contained roughly 14 tropical storms, seven hurricanes, three major hurricanes, and an [accumulated cyclone energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accumulated_cyclone_energy "Accumulated cyclone energy") (ACE) index of 74–126 units.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Dec21TSR-27) Broadly speaking, ACE is a measure of the power of a tropical or subtropical storm multiplied by the length of time it existed. It is only calculated for full advisories on specific tropical and subtropical systems reaching or exceeding wind speeds of 39 mph (63 km/h).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Background-6) NOAA typically categorizes a season as above-average, average, or below-average based on the cumulative ACE index, but the number of tropical storms, hurricanes, and major hurricanes within a hurricane season is sometimes also considered.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Background-6)

### Pre-season forecasts

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Pre-season forecasts")]

On December 9, 2021, CSU issued an extended-range forecast for the 2022 hurricane season, giving a 40% chance of near-average activity with 13–16 named storms, 6–8 hurricanes, 2–3 major hurricanes, and an ACE index of about 130 units. The forecast also gave a 25% chance that the ACE Index would end up being around 170 units, and a 25% likelihood the likelihood that the index would end up around 80.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Dec21CSU-8) TSR also issued an extended-range forecast on December 10, 2021.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Dec22TSR-9) It predicted overall near-average tropical activity with its ACE index, anticipating 18 tropical storms, 8 hurricanes, and 3 intense hurricanes to form during the season. One of their factors was the expectation of a neutral [El Niño-Southern Oscillation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Ni%C3%B1o-Southern_Oscillation "El Niño-Southern Oscillation") condition by the third quarter of 2022. This outlook had "large uncertainties".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Dec22TSR-9)

In their April 6, 2022, forecast, TSR's number of named storms remained unchanged, while they slightly increased the number of major hurricane from three to four.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Apr6TSR-10) On the following day, CSU issued their first extended-range seasonal forecast for the 2022 Atlantic hurricane season, predicting well-above-average activity, with 19 named storms, 9 hurricanes, 4 major hurricanes, and an ACE index of 160 units. Their factors supporting an active hurricane season included above average-sea surface temperatures in the subtropical Atlantic Ocean and Caribbean Sea, and a cool neutral ENSO or weak La Niña pattern, corresponding to a low chance of an [El Niño](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Ni%C3%B1o "El Niño").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Apr7CSU-11)[The Weather Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Weather_Channel "The Weather Channel") (TWC) issued their first seasonal forecast on April 14, calling for 20 named storms, 8 hurricanes, and 4 major hurricanes.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Apr14TWC-12) On the same day, the [University of Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Arizona "University of Arizona") (UA) issued its seasonal prediction for a slightly above-average hurricane season, with 14 named storms, 7 hurricanes, 3 major hurricanes, and an ACE index of 129 units.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Apr14UA-13)[North Carolina State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina_State_University "North Carolina State University") (NCSU) made its prediction for the season on April 20, calling for an above-average season with 17 to 21 named storms, 7 to 9 hurricanes, and 3 to 5 major hurricanes.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Apr20NCSU-14)

On May 9, [Pennsylvania State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_State_University "Pennsylvania State University") predicted 14.9 +/- 3.8 tropical storms, or a range of 11 to 19 named storms.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-pennstate-15) On May 23, UKMO issued their own forecast for the 2022 season, predicting an above-average season with 18 named storms, 9 hurricanes, and 4 major hurricanes, with a 70% chance that each of these statistics will fall between 13 and 23, 6 and 12, and 2 and 6, respectively.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-May23UKMO-16) The following day, NOAA's Climate Prediction Center issued their forecasts for the season, predicting a 65% chance of above-average activity and 25% chance for below-average activity, with 14–21 named storms, 6–10 hurricanes, and 3–6 major hurricanes.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-May24NOAA-17) TSR released another prediction on May 31 that was unchanged from its April 6 forecast: 18 named storms, 8 hurricanes, and 4 major hurricanes.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-May31TSR-18)

### Mid-season forecasts

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mid-season forecasts")]

On June 2, CSU updated their extended-range seasonal forecast, increasing the amount of tropical cyclones to 20 named storms, 10 hurricanes, 5 major hurricanes, and an overall ACE index of 180 units. This was done after a later analysis of the lower chances of an El Niño during the season, as well as a warmer-than-average tropical Atlantic.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Jun2CSU-19) TWC's second outlook, released on June 17, slightly increased the number of named storms to 21 and hurricanes to 9, but left the number of major hurricanes at 4.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Jun17TWC-20) On June 20, 2022, UA updated its seasonal prediction, which is very similar to its April prediction, with 15 named storms, 7 hurricanes, 3 major hurricanes, and an ACE index of 131 units.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Jun20UA-21) On July 5, TSR released their third forecast for the season, slightly increasing their numbers to 18 named storms, 9 hurricanes, and 4 major hurricanes. This prediction was largely based on the persistence of the weak La Niña into the third quarter of the year.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Jul5TSR-22) On July 7, CSU did not make changes to their updated prediction of 20 named storms, 10 hurricanes, and 5 major hurricanes.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Jul7CSU-23) UKMO's updated forecast on August 2 called for 16 named storms, 6 hurricanes, and 4 major hurricanes.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Aug2UKMO-24) Two days later, NOAA and CSU each revised their activity outlook slightly downward, though both still predicted that the season would end up being busier than the 30-year average. The revisions were made in part because of the relative slow start to the season (as compared to the past few years), with only three short-lived named storms as of the start of August.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-EOTS8422-25) The third and final TWC seasonal forecast, issued on August 18, decreased the number of named storms to 17, hurricanes to 7, and major hurricanes to 3.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Aug18TWC-26)

### Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Background")]

[![Image 7: A satellite photo of Tropical Storm Earl (bottom left) and Hurricane Danielle (top right) both active simultaneously on September 5, 2022.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/Danielle_and_Earl_on_September_5_2022.jpg/250px-Danielle_and_Earl_on_September_5_2022.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Danielle_and_Earl_on_September_5_2022.jpg)

[Tropical Storm Earl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Earl_(2022) "Hurricane Earl (2022)") (bottom left) and Hurricane Danielle (top right) on September 5

Officially, the 2022 Atlantic hurricane season ran from June 1 to November 30.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-pennstate-15) A total of 16 tropical cyclones developed, 14 of which intensified into named storms. Of those, eight strengthened into a hurricane, while two systems reached major hurricane intensity. Thus, the season was near-average compared to NOAA's 1991–2020 mean of 14 named storms, 7 hurricanes, and 3 major hurricanes.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-TWSAT_1122-2) The near-average number of named storms ended the record six-year streak of above-average activity in the Atlantic.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-bizarre-28) A strong La Niña and slightly above-normal West African Monsoon season led to the mostly average activity. However, intense wind shear and the suppression of moisture in the atmosphere by the [Saharan Air Layer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saharan_Air_Layer "Saharan Air Layer") led to an unusual mid-season cessation in tropical cyclogenesis that lasted nearly two months,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-noaa_11/29-29)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-30) with no named storms in the Atlantic between July 3 and August 31 for the first time since [1941](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1941_Atlantic_hurricane_season "1941 Atlantic hurricane season").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-bizarre-28)

Hurricanes [Fiona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Fiona "Hurricane Fiona") and [Ian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Ian "Hurricane Ian") inflicted historically significant impacts on certain areas. After Fiona caused a few billion dollars in damage in Puerto Rico, its remnants struck [Nova Scotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nova_Scotia "Nova Scotia") as a powerful [extratropical cyclone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extratropical_cyclone "Extratropical cyclone"), becoming the costliest weather disaster on record in [Atlantic Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Canada "Atlantic Canada").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Fiona_TCR-31) Ian became both the costliest Florida hurricane and the third-costliest on record in the United States, behind only [Hurricane Katrina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Katrina "Hurricane Katrina") in [2005](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2005 Atlantic hurricane season") and [Hurricane Harvey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Harvey "Hurricane Harvey") in [2017](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2017 Atlantic hurricane season"). Additionally, 150 fatalities occurred in Florida,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-:1-32) making Ian the deadliest tropical cyclone in the state since the [1935 Labor Day hurricane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1935_Labor_Day_hurricane "1935 Labor Day hurricane").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-bizarre-28) Collectively, the tropical cyclones of the 2022 Atlantic hurricane season caused at least 304 fatalities and more than $117.708 billion in damage,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-atcr-33) making it one of the costliest seasons of all time.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-EOTS_1110-34)

This season's [ACE index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accumulated_cyclone_energy "Accumulated cyclone energy") was approximately 94.6 units,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-35) which was 77% of the long-term (30-year) average of 123.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-TWSAT_1122-2) This was the first season since [2007](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2007 Atlantic hurricane season") to have an ACE value that is near-average. All seasons from 2008 to 2021 were either below or above-average.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Apr7CSU-11)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9c/Fiona%2C_Gaston%2C_Hermine_and_09L_on_September_23%2C_2022.png/250px-Fiona%2C_Gaston%2C_Hermine_and_09L_on_September_23%2C_2022.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fiona,_Gaston,_Hermine_and_09L_on_September_23,_2022.png)

Four tropical cyclones active simultaneously on September 23: [Hurricane Fiona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Fiona "Hurricane Fiona") (top-left), Tropical Storm Gaston (top-right), [Tropical Storm Hermine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Hermine_(2022) "Tropical Storm Hermine (2022)") (bottom-right), and Tropical Depression Nine (bottom-left, which ultimately became [Hurricane Ian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Ian "Hurricane Ian")). The wave that would later spawn Tropical Depression Eleven can be seen to the left of Hermine.

Overall, [NOAA Hurricane Hunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NOAA_Hurricane_Hunters "NOAA Hurricane Hunters") logged more than 582 flight hours while conducting 65 eyewall passages and deploying more than 1,700 scientific instruments, including [dropsondes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropsonde "Dropsonde"). Additionally, the Gulfstream IV-SP took off from the Cabo Verde Islands in August, becoming the easternmost hurricane hunter flight. NOAA also launched an [Altius-600](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altius-600 "Altius-600") for the first time, which recorded wind speed data on Hurricane Ian as it approached landfall in Florida. Crews of flights conducted by the [National Ocean Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Ocean_Service "National Ocean Service") took thousands of aerial images of the destruction caused by Ian, which especially assisted with identifying pollutants and areas requiring extensive [marine debris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_debris "Marine debris") cleanup. NOAA's King Air and Twin Otter aircraft were also involved in a similar mission in the aftermath of Ian and Hurricane Nicole, logging more than 41 flight hours.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-noaa_11/29-29)

### Early season activity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Early season activity")]

The 2022 season was the first since [2014](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2014 Atlantic hurricane season") to not have a pre-season named storm. Activity began with the formation of [Tropical Storm Alex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Alex_(2022) "Tropical Storm Alex (2022)") on June 5, after several days of slow development while traversing the [Gulf of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Mexico "Gulf of Mexico") and then moving over Central Florida.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-36) The storm peaked at near-hurricane strength before becoming extratropical on the following day over the Central North Atlantic. On July 1, [Tropical Storm Bonnie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Bonnie_(2022) "Hurricane Bonnie (2022)") formed in the Southern [Caribbean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean_Sea "Caribbean Sea") and made landfall shortly thereafter near the Costa Rica–Nicaragua border. It then [crossed over](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Atlantic%E2%80%93Pacific_crossover_hurricanes "List of Atlantic–Pacific crossover hurricanes") into the Pacific basin a day later, the first storm to do so since [Hurricane Otto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Otto "Hurricane Otto") in [2016](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2016 Atlantic hurricane season"),[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-37) where it would become a Category 3 hurricane.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-btcr-38) Also on July 1, a low-pressure system off the U.S. Atlantic coast near [Savannah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savannah,_Georgia "Savannah, Georgia"), [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)"), abruptly organized into Tropical Storm Colin, a short-lived storm that dissipated the next day inland over northeastern South Carolina.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Colin_TCR-39) Tropical cyclogenesis then ceased for almost two months, with 2022 becoming the first season since [1997](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Atlantic_hurricane_season "1997 Atlantic hurricane season") in which no tropical cyclones formed in August.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-EOTS_83122-40) A disturbance over the Gulf of Mexico was briefly designated as a _potential tropical cyclone_ during the month, but it did not organize into a tropical cyclone before moving inland over Northeastern [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-PTC4TCR-41)

Tropical activity ultimately resumed with the formation of Tropical Storm Danielle over the central Atlantic on September 1. The storm intensified into a hurricane the following day, the latest first hurricane since [2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2013 Atlantic hurricane season").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-42) It remained nearly stationary far to the west of the [Azores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azores "Azores") for several days before moving northeastward and becoming extratropical on September 8 without affecting any land areas.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-dtcr-43) Additionally, a slow-developing disturbance east of the [Lesser Antilles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lesser_Antilles "Lesser Antilles") became organized and developed into Tropical Storm Earl late on September 2. It strengthened into a hurricane, tracked east of [Bermuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bermuda "Bermuda"), fluctuating between Category 1 and 2 intensity, and then became extratropical near [Newfoundland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newfoundland_(island) "Newfoundland (island)") on September 10.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-etcr-44) Four days later, Tropical Storm Fiona formed in the Central Atlantic. Fiona eventually became a hurricane, striking both [Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Rico "Puerto Rico") and the [Dominican Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominican_Republic "Dominican Republic") before becoming the season's first major hurricane as it passed by the [Turks and Caicos Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turks_and_Caicos_Islands "Turks and Caicos Islands") on September 20. That same day, Tropical Storm Gaston formed over the Central Atlantic and moved through the Western Azores. Fiona strengthened into a Category 4 hurricane as it passed west of Bermuda and transitioned into a powerful extratropical cyclone on September 23, just before striking Nova Scotia.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Fiona_TCR-31) That same day, Tropical Depression Nine formed in the Caribbean Sea and Tropical Depression Ten formed in the eastern tropical Atlantic, marking the first time since [2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2020 Atlantic hurricane season") that four tropical cyclones were active simultaneously in the Atlantic basin.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-YCC_092422-45)

Tropical Depression Nine became [Hurricane Ian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Ian "Hurricane Ian"), the deadliest and most destructive storm of the season. Ian made landfall in western Cuba and crossed the [Florida Keys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Keys "Florida Keys") as a Category 3 hurricane, before briefly becoming a Category 5 hurricane. It then made landfall in southwestern Florida as a high-end Category 4 hurricane, with winds of 150 mph (240 km/h), the strongest storm to hit the area in terms of windspeed. The storm later made landfall in South Carolina as a Category 1.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-:1-32) Tropical Depression Ten attained tropical storm strength first, becoming [Tropical Storm Hermine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Hermine_(2022) "Tropical Storm Hermine (2022)").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Hermine_TCR-46) It was one of the easternmost Atlantic tropical storms on record,[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-YCC_92222-47) and brought heavy rainfall to the [Canary Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Islands "Canary Islands").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Hermine_TCR-46) Next, Tropical Depression Eleven formed during the last week in September, and then Tropical Depression Twelve formed one week later. Ultimately, neither cyclone strengthened into a tropical storm.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-11tcr-48)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-12tcr-49) Soon thereafter, [Hurricane Julia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Julia_(2022) "Hurricane Julia (2022)") formed just off the coast of [Venezuela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venezuela "Venezuela") on October 7. After traversing Nicaragua intact, Julia entered the Pacific basin.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-jtcr-50) Not since [1996](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Atlantic_hurricane_season "1996 Atlantic hurricane season") has more than one storm crossed between the Atlantic and Pacific basins intact during a single season.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Henson_EOTS-51) On October 11, Tropical Storm Karl formed in the [Bay of Campeche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_of_Campeche "Bay of Campeche"), moved erratically over open waters, before degenerating into a remnant low offshore of Mexico three days later.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Karl_TCR-52) Hurricane Martin was the second largest Atlantic hurricane on record as measured by diameter, behind km).[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-53)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-54) Martin and [Lisa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Lisa_(2022) "Hurricane Lisa (2022)") were both at hurricane strength on November 2, thus, for the first time since with three.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-bizarre-28) Nicole impacted the [Greater Antilles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Antilles "Greater Antilles"), the [Bahamas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahamas "Bahamas"), and the [Eastern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_United_States "Eastern United States"), becoming the ### Tropical Storm Alex

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Tropical Storm Alex")]

Tropical storm(SSHWS)
[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/Alex_2022-06-05_2210Z.png/250px-Alex_2022-06-05_2210Z.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alex_2022-06-05_2210Z.png)[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e8/Alex_2022_path.png/250px-Alex_2022_path.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alex_2022_path.png)
Duration June 5– June 6
Peak intensity 70 mph (110 km/h) (1-min);  
984[mbar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_(unit) "Bar (unit)")([hPa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pascal_(unit) "Pascal (unit)"))

Main article: [Tropical Storm Alex (2022)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Alex_(2022) "Tropical Storm Alex (2022)")

In late May, the mid-level remnants of [Hurricane Agatha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Agatha "Hurricane Agatha") in the Pacific basin interacted with a Central American Gyre. Consequently, a gradual increase in deep [convection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_convection "Atmospheric convection") occurred over the [Yucatán Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yucat%C3%A1n_Peninsula "Yucatán Peninsula") and the northwestern Caribbean Sea, which led to the development of a [low-pressure area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low-pressure_area "Low-pressure area") just north of the [Belize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belize "Belize")-Mexico border on June 2. After emerging into the southeastern Gulf of Mexico early the next day, the disturbance made multiple attempts at organizing into a tropical cyclone and attained tropical storm-force winds. However, strong [wind shear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_shear "Wind shear") kept the system disorganized before it struck [Southwest Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwest_Florida "Southwest Florida") on June 4. Several hours later, the disturbance emerged into the Atlantic, where it developed into Tropical Storm Alex at 00:00[UTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time "Coordinated Universal Time") on June 5 about 85 mi (135 km) north of [Grand Bahama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Bahama "Grand Bahama"). Additional intensification occurred as Alex moved east-northeastward due to mid-latitude westerly flow, reaching sustained winds of 70 mph (110 km/h) around 18:00 UTC. However, drier air caused Alex to weaken on the following day, with the storm transitioning into an extratropical cyclone at 12:00 UTC roughly 105 mi (170 km) north-northwest of Bermuda. The remnants of Alex were absorbed by a baroclinic zone early on June 7.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-atcr-33)

Due to the threat the developing system posed to [Cuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuba "Cuba"), the [Florida Keys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Keys "Florida Keys"), and [South Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Florida "South Florida"), the [National Hurricane Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Hurricane_Center "National Hurricane Center") initiated advisories on it, designating it as _[Potential Tropical Cyclone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary\_of\_tropical\_cyclone\_terms#P "Glossary of tropical cyclone terms") One_. The precursor to Alex dropped heavy precipitation in these regions.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-atcr-33) During a 30-hour period on June 2–3, Paso Real de San Diego in the province of [Pinar del Río](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinar_del_R%C3%ADo_Province "Pinar del Río Province") recorded about 12 inches (301 mm) of rain, and [Playa Girón](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playa_Gir%C3%B3n "Playa Girón") in [Matanzas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matanzas_Province "Matanzas Province") received over 8 inches (193 mm).[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-57) There were four storm-related deaths in Cuba, while about 750 homes, 7,900 [acres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acre "Acre") (3,200[ha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hectare "Hectare")) of crops,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-atcr-33) and numerous bridges suffered flood damage.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-58) According to AON, damages from flooding totaled at least US$25 million in Cuba.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-:2-59) In Florida, several locations in the Upper Keys and the [Miami metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_metropolitan_area "Miami metropolitan area") observed between 10 and 15 in (250 and 380 mm) of rainfall, with a peak total of 15.28 in (388 mm) near [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood,_Florida "Hollywood, Florida"). Extensive street flooding occurred in the Miami area, but water entered only a few properties. Across [Broward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broward_County,_Florida "Broward County, Florida") and [Miami-Dade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami-Dade_County,_Florida "Miami-Dade County, Florida") counties combined, there were about 3,500 power outages.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-atcr-33) Damage from the precursor to Alex in Florida totaled $104,000.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-NCDCAlex-60) However, it was later determined that flood damages in Florida were more than $350 million.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-:2-59)

### Tropical Storm Bonnie

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Tropical Storm Bonnie")]

Main article: [Hurricane Bonnie (2022)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Bonnie_(2022) "Hurricane Bonnie (2022)")

A low-altitude tropical wave entered the Atlantic from the west coast of Africa on June 22, producing a large but disorganized area of showers and thunderstorms. Thunderstorm activity increased by June 27, while a NOAA Hurricane Hunters mission reported tropical-storm-force winds but no well-defined closed circulation. However, due to the threat the system posed to the Lesser Antilles, the NHC initiated advisories on it as _Potential Tropical Cyclone Two_ later that same day. Later, after crossing the southern Windward Islands on June 28 and passing near the coast of Venezuela on the following day, the disturbance encountered more favorable conditions but failed to develop a distinct low-level circulation due to its fast forward speed and interaction with land. As the disturbance moved toward [Central America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_America "Central America") on the morning of July 1, it became sufficiently organized to be classified as Tropical Storm Bonnie.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-btcr-38) Embedded in an environment of low wind shear and warm seas, Bonnie started to steadily intensify.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-61) At 03:00 UTC on July 2, Bonnie made landfall near the Costa Rica–Nicaragua border at its peak intensity within the Atlantic with sustained winds of 60 mph (95 km/h). Bonnie then crossed Central America and exited into the Eastern Pacific basin around 12:00 UTC on July 2.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-btcr-38)

Bonnie and its precursor disturbance produced gusty winds and heavy rainfall as it tracked through the southern Caribbean.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-YCC_62922-62) On [Trinidad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinidad "Trinidad"), floodwaters damaged at least 40 homes in one village and left approximately 200,000 people without potable water.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-btcr-38) Heavy rainfall and landslides in [Panama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama "Panama") led to the evacuation of several families in [Chiriquí Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiriqu%C3%AD_Province "Chiriquí Province").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-63) In [Costa Rica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica "Costa Rica"), over 3,000 people evacuated as a result of flooding and mudslides,[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-btcr-38) while 8,593 households lost electricity.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-64) Over 10,000 people lost power during the storm in [Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua "Nicaragua"). Four deaths occurred in the country, three after being swept away in rising rivers and one while attempting to rescue other people from a bus being carried away. Overall, Bonnie caused about $25 million in damage throughout the impacted regions.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-btcr-38)

A low-pressure area formed along a surface trough offshore Savannah, Georgia, on July 1. The system then unexpectedly organized into a tropical depression around 18:00 UTC that day, and strengthened into Tropical Storm Colin at 23:30 UTC as it made landfall near [Hunting Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunting_Island_State_Park "Hunting Island State Park"), South Carolina. Simultaneously, Colin peaked with maximum sustained winds of 40 mph (65 km/h). The center of the storm remained just inland over coastal South Carolina on July 2, though most of its heavy rains and strong winds remained out over the Atlantic due to its proximity to the coast and wind shear.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Colin_TCR-39) Colin became increasingly disorganized later that day, with its circulation becoming elongated due to the wind shear and continued land interaction.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-65) By 18:00 UTC on July 2, Colin had fallen to tropical depression intensity. The storm continued to weaken rapidly, and its low-level circulation dissipated over northeastern South Carolina by the end of that day.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Colin_TCR-39)

A few locations from Northeast Florida to Southeastern North Carolina observed 3 to 4 in (76 to 102 mm) of precipitation. In South Carolina, rainfall amounts ranged from 1–3 in (25–76 mm) in parts of the [Midlands region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midlands_of_South_Carolina "Midlands of South Carolina") to a peak total of 7.59 in (193 mm) near [Wadmalaw Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wadmalaw_Island "Wadmalaw Island").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Colin_TCR-39) A [Fourth of July](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independence_Day_(United_States) "Independence Day (United States)") weekend event in Charleston was cancelled because of flooding at the event site, as was a festival in [Southport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southport,_North_Carolina "Southport, North Carolina"), North Carolina.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-66) However, only minor damage occurred overall. One person drowned at [Oak Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oak_Island,_North_Carolina "Oak Island, North Carolina"), North Carolina, due to rip currents generated by Colin.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Colin_TCR-39)

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/30/Danielle_2022-09-05_1020Z.jpg/250px-Danielle_2022-09-05_1020Z.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Danielle_2022-09-05_1020Z.jpg)[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/Danielle_2022_path.png/250px-Danielle_2022_path.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Danielle_2022_path.png)

Peak intensity 85 mph (140 km/h) (1-min);  
972[mbar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_(unit) "Bar (unit)")([hPa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pascal_(unit) "Pascal (unit)"))

On August 31, an area of low pressure formed along a decaying frontal zone over the central subtropical Atlantic. The disturbance quickly developed into Tropical Depression Five early on September 1 roughly 715 mi (1,150 km) southeast of [Cape Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Race "Cape Race"), [Newfoundland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newfoundland_and_Labrador "Newfoundland and Labrador"), before strengthening into Tropical Storm Danielle by 12:00 UTC. Favorable conditions such as abnormally warm seas and light wind shear allowed Danielle to become a hurricane around 24 hours later. The hurricane stalled on September 2, caught south of a blocking high, and weakened back to a tropical storm the next day due to [upwelling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upwelling "Upwelling") of cooler waters. Later, the storm drifted westward, where it again strengthened into a hurricane early on September 4. After turning northwestward, Danielle reached its peak intensity with sustained winds of 85 mph (140 km/h) late the following day.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-dtcr-43) It then moved over a relatively cool part of the [Gulf Stream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Stream "Gulf Stream") and weakened to a low-end Category 1 hurricane.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-67) The hurricane briefly re-intensified when it moved over marginally warm waters on September 7, but resumed a weakening trend shortly thereafter.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-68) Danielle weakened to a tropical storm early on September 8, before transitioning into an extratropical cyclone later that day. The remnant extratropical system meandered over the northeastern Atlantic before dissipating offshore [Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal "Portugal") on September 15.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-dtcr-43)

The remnants of Danielle dissipated offshore Portugal as an extratropical cyclone, bringing heavy rain to the country, including 3.3 in (84 mm) of precipitation in [Guarda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guarda,_Portugal "Guarda, Portugal") in 24 hours.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-dtcr-43) Between September 12–13, 644 accidents were reported throughout the country, along with many instances of downed trees and flash floods.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-:0-69) One man was hospitalized after he was swept away by floodwaters.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-70) In [Manteigas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manteigas "Manteigas"), which had been ravaged by intense summer forest fires in nearby areas of the [Serra da Estrela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serra_da_Estrela "Serra da Estrela") mountain range, floods and landslides caused major damage and at least four vehicles were dragged into the [Zêzere River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z%C3%AAzere_River "Zêzere River"). Portuguese authorities also reported minor wind and flood damage in Lisbon and [Setúbal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set%C3%BAbal "Setúbal").[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-71) Much of [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain") was put on yellow alert as wind, rain and thunderstorms triggered by the cyclone moved inland.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-72)

### Hurricane Earl

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Hurricane Earl")]

Category 2 hurricane(SSHWS)
[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/Earl_2022-09-10_0515Z_%28Colored%29.jpg/250px-Earl_2022-09-10_0515Z_%28Colored%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Earl_2022-09-10_0515Z_(Colored).jpg)[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/97/Earl_2022_path.png/250px-Earl_2022_path.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Earl_2022_path.png)
Duration September 2– September 10
Peak intensity 110 mph (175 km/h) (1-min);  
948[mbar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_(unit) "Bar (unit)")([hPa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pascal_(unit) "Pascal (unit)"))

Main article: [Hurricane Earl (2022)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Earl_(2022) "Hurricane Earl (2022)")

On August 25, a tropical wave emerged into the Atlantic from the west coast of Africa. Convective activity remained sporadic and disorganized for several days as the wave moved generally west-northwestward through an environment of dry air and unfavorable wind shear. However, convection markedly increased on September 1 as the system approached warm waters near the Lesser Antilles. Late on the following day, the system organized into Tropical Storm Earl approximately 205 mi (330 km) east of [Barbuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbuda "Barbuda"). Continuously unconducive wind shear prevented significant intensification before Earl turned northward on September 5 through a break in a subtropical ridge over the central Atlantic. Possibly due to a diffluent environment and favorable thermodynamic conditions, Earl intensified into a hurricane late on September 6. The storm briefly strengthened into a Category 2 hurricane early on September 8 but then weakened later that day, likely due to dry air.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-etcr-44)

Around 12:00 UTC on September 9, Earl re-strengthened into a Category 2 hurricane. About 12 hours later, the hurricane peaked with sustained winds of 110 mph (175 km/h) and a minimum barometric pressure of 948 mbar (28.0 inHg) as it accelerated northeastward in advance of a mid-latitude trough. However, Earl soon began losing tropical characteristics and transitioned into an extratropical cyclone around 18:00 UTC on September 10, about 230 mi (370 km) south of Cape Race, Newfoundland. The extratropical remnants executed a cyclonic loop south of Newfoundland before moving generally eastward across the Atlantic before dissipating late on September 15.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-etcr-44)

The outerbands of Earl produced rainfall amounts generally ranging from 3 to 5 in (76 to 127 mm) in eastern Puerto Rico, while a weather station near Finca La Loma recorded a peak total of 7.7 in (200 mm) of precipitation. Two people died near [Salinas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salinas,_Puerto_Rico "Salinas, Puerto Rico") after being struck by lightning while riding a jet ski. Bermuda was buffeted with sustained winds of 35 mph (60 km/h) as Hurricane Earl passed within about 90 mi (145 km) of the island's eastern coast; higher gusts were reported, including one of 67 mph (108 km/h) at the [National Museum of Bermuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_Bermuda "National Museum of Bermuda").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-etcr-44) There were localized power outages across the archipelago but no large-scale damage was observed.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Gazette-2-73) During a 36-hour period September 10–12,7–8 in (175–200 mm) of rain fell in the [St. Johns area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._John's,_Newfoundland_and_Labrador "St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador") of Newfoundland and Labrador,[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Earl-Avalon-74) causing the Waterford River to overflow, which led to [urban flooding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_flooding "Urban flooding"). Similar rainfall amounts were also reported in communities throughout the [Avalon Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avalon_Peninsula "Avalon Peninsula"). Additionally, the cyclone generated rough surf which damaged the breakwater on the coast in the area of [Trepassey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trepassey "Trepassey"), causing localized flooding.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-etcr-44)

### Hurricane Fiona

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Hurricane Fiona")]

Category 4 hurricane(SSHWS)
[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/Fiona_2022-09-22_2131Z.jpg/250px-Fiona_2022-09-22_2131Z.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fiona_2022-09-22_2131Z.jpg)[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/Fiona_2022_path.png/250px-Fiona_2022_path.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fiona_2022_path.png)
Duration September 14– September 23
Peak intensity 140 mph (220 km/h) (1-min);  
931[mbar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_(unit) "Bar (unit)")([hPa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pascal_(unit) "Pascal (unit)"))

Main article: [Hurricane Fiona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Fiona "Hurricane Fiona")

A tropical wave exited the west coast of Africa and entered the Atlantic on September 7. Although shower and thunderstorm activity was initially organized, dry air significantly limited convection as the wave trekked westward for several days. However, convection began increasing on September 12 and consolidating late on September 13. A well-defined circulation formed early the following day, leading to the development of a tropical depression approximately 1,035 mi (1,665 km) east of the Lesser Antilles. Although the depression strengthened into Tropical Storm Fiona later on September 14, wind shear prevented further significant intensification for a few days as the storm continued to move generally westward. Late on September 16, Fiona struck [Guadeloupe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guadeloupe "Guadeloupe") with winds of 60 mph (95 km/h). After entering the Caribbean, the cyclone encountered decreasing wind shear, allowing it to intensify into a hurricane on September 18. At 19:20 UTC, Fiona made landfall in the [Lajas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lajas,_Puerto_Rico "Lajas, Puerto Rico") municipality of Puerto Rico near Punta Tocon with winds of 85 mph (140 km/h). The storm quickly emerged into the [Mona Passage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mona_Passage "Mona Passage") and moved west-northwestward until striking the Dominican Republic near [Boca de Yuma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boca_de_Yuma "Boca de Yuma") with winds of 90 mph (150 km/h) around 07:30 UTC on September 19.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Fiona_TCR-31)

Fiona emerged into the Atlantic from the north coast of the Dominican Republic later on September 19 and soon intensified into a Category 2 hurricane. The storm then reached Category 3 intensity early on the following day, prior to striking [Grand Turk Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Turk_Island "Grand Turk Island") around 11:00 UTC. Thereafter, Fiona moved north-northeastward due to a weakness in the subtropical ridge and strengthened into a Category 4 hurricane early on September 21. At that time, the cyclone peaked with sustained winds of 140 mph (220 km/h). Although sustained winds then decreased slightly, the storm's minimum pressure fell to 931 mbar (27.5 inHg) early on September 23. Fiona also expanded significantly that day while passing about 115 mi (185 km) northwest of Bermuda around 10:00 UTC. The storm accelerated northeastward and then north-northeastward while merging with a cold front several hours later, with Fiona becoming extratropical by 00:00 UTC on September 24 approximately 220 mi (355 km) southeast of [Halifax, Nova Scotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax,_Nova_Scotia "Halifax, Nova Scotia"). The remnants of Fiona remained intense and struck Nova Scotia around 07:00 UTC that day and then extreme eastern [Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec "Quebec") on September 25, several hours before reaching the [Labrador Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labrador_Sea "Labrador Sea"). The extratropical cyclone dissipated just offshore [Nuuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuuk "Nuuk"), [Greenland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland "Greenland"), late on September 27.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Fiona_TCR-31)

Several of the [Leeward Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leeward_Islands "Leeward Islands") recorded tropical storm-force winds and heavy rainfall, with up to 22.22 in (564 mm) of precipitation on Guadeloupe, leading to one death after the overflowing [Rivière des Pères](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rivi%C3%A8re%20des%20P%C3%A8res "fr:Rivière des Pères") swept away a house.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Fiona_TCR-31) Still recovering from the [effects of Hurricane Maria in 2017](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effects_of_Hurricane_Maria_in_Puerto_Rico "Effects of Hurricane Maria in Puerto Rico") and saturated from precipitation produced by Earl,[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-YCC_91822-75) torrential rains fell island-wide on Puerto Rico on September 18–19, exceeding 30 in (760 mm) in some regions, causing destructive flash flooding, landslides, and rockfalls that washed out or blocked numerous roads and bridges. In addition, the effects of the storm resulted in an island-wide power grid failure. A loss of approximately 90% of commercial crops also occurred. Overall, Fiona caused 23 deaths and about $2.5 billion in damage in Puerto Rico, making Fiona the island's third costliest tropical cyclone on record. In the Dominican Republic, heavy rainfall and hurricane-force winds destroyed more than 2,000 homes and damaged about 8,500 others, displacing over 43,000 people. More than 400,000 people lost electricity and 1.2 million people experienced a disruption of water services. Two deaths occurred in the country,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Fiona_TCR-31) while damage totaled approximately $375 million.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-sanchez-76) In the Turks and Caicos Islands, strong winds downed many trees and power poles and damaged some homes. Similar impacts were reported in Bermuda, along with approximately 29,000 customers losing electricity. In Atlantic Canada, strong winds felled thousands of power lines and trees across the region, leaving over 500,000 customers without electricity and causing significant damage to roofs and windows in Nova Scotia. Large waves and [storm surge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_surge "Storm surge") demolished more than 100 homes in southwestern Newfoundland and flooded many dwellings and businesses on the [Magdalen Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magdalen_Islands "Magdalen Islands"). Eight deaths were reported in Atlantic Canada, while insured losses alone reached $800 million, making the remnants of Fiona the costliest weather disaster in the region's history.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season#cite_note-Fiona_TCR-31)

### Tropical Storm Gaston

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2022_Atlantic_hurricane_season&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Tropical Storm Gaston")]

Tropical storm(SSHWS)
[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/46/Gaston_2022-09-22_1525Z.jpg/250px-Gaston_2022-09-22_1525Z.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gaston_2022-09-22_1525Z.jpg)[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/Gaston_2022_path.png/250px-Gaston_2022_path.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gaston_2022_path.png)
